title: Royce White shows up to Indiana Fever game in blonde wig amid WNBA Draft pursuit
excerpt:
Former NBA player and men's college basketball star Royce White arrived at Gainbridge Fieldhouse Friday night wearing a wig more than a week after he declared for the WNBA Draft.

Former NBA player Ro...
body_text:
Former NBA player and men's college basketball star Royce White arrived at Gainbridge Fieldhouse Friday night wearing a wig more than a week after he declared for the WNBA Draft.

Former NBA player Royce White brought his WNBA Draft campaign directly to an arena Friday night, just days after Enes Kanter Freedom was thrown out of a game. Both White and Freedom have declared for the next WNBA Draft as males.

White attended the Indiana Fever’s game against the Connecticut Sun at Gainbridge Fieldhouse wearing a long blonde wig, as seen in photos and video obtained by OutKick.

The former first-round NBA pick could be seen inside the arena wearing the wig as the Fever prepared to take on Connecticut. He was greeted with a friendly welcome by fans, as multiple people stopped to shake his hand and take pictures with him.

Royce White at Gainbridge Fieldhouse (OutKick)

FORMER NBA PLAYER ROYCE WHITE SAYS HE IS DECLARING FOR NEXT WNBA DRAFT AFTER ENES KANTER ANNOUNCEMENT

When asked by OutKick why he was there, White said, "All hail Queen Roysha, the queen has arrived, it's great to be here... I'm here because Black trans lesbians matter, and we've always mattered, we've always existed... I'm here to participate and scout some of the competition maybe as well."

Freedom’s ejection became a national storyline Sunday night and continued to draw attention after he was banned from future Sky games.

CHICAGO SKY OWNER OPENS UP ON ENES KANTER FREEDOM EJECTION, MAKES ANALOGY TO SHOOTING A GUN

When asked about Freedom's incident and if fans might also see some "fireworks" with White in attendance on Friday, White responded, "I'm just here to spectate. I'm just here to support the WNBA and support the Fever."

Royce White shakes hands with a fan at Gainbridge Fieldhouse (OutKick)

Asked what reception he expected from Fever fans Friday, White was unfazed:

"Who cares? It’s life, you get one life to live. You’re born, you breathe, you stop breathing, hopefully you give all glory to God … Who cares what the reaction is?"

His appearance continued the public campaign he launched earlier this month when he announced his intention to enter the 2027 WNBA Draft.

White previously previewed the look on social media.

White formally declared for the draft in a letter sent to the WNBA league office by his attorney, former Florida congressman Matt Gaetz. The declaration stated that White identified as a transgender woman and claimed eligibility under the league’s new collective bargaining agreement.

The CBA states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA," but it does not provide a more specific definition based on biological sex or gender identity.

White has made clear that his declaration is intended to pressure the WNBA into explicitly stating whether biological males can compete in the league.

"I’m transgender. I’m a woman. I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball, professional basketball, so I’ll be declaring for the WNBA draft in 2027 as well," White previously told OutKick.

White has also threatened to pursue a discrimination lawsuit if he is not allowed to compete.

Multiple outlets reported this week that White and fellow former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom would not be eligible for the draft. A league source characterized their declarations as "publicity stunts." However, White’s legal team said it had not received a formal determination directly from the WNBA.

Royce White poses with a fan before a WNBA game in Indiana.  (OutKick)

"The WNBA should preserve all records in anticipation of litigation," Gaetz wrote on social media.

White was selected by the Houston Rockets with the 16th overall pick in the 2012 NBA Draft after starring at Iowa State. He appeared in only three NBA games, all with the Sacramento Kings in 2014.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

title: US revises statements suggesting Chinese hackers attacked agencies
excerpt: United States officials have corrected earlier statements that several government agencies were attacked by Chinese hackers, now saying instead that the organisations were only among the hackers’ targ...
body_text:
United States officials have corrected earlier statements that several government agencies were attacked by Chinese hackers, now saying instead that the organisations were only among the hackers’ targets.

In a newly edited statement on Friday, the US Department of Justice said that the Senate, the Federal Reserve, NASA and other agencies were “among the targets of QTFY”, a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group.

A previous version of the statement said the government agencies had been among the hackers’ victims.

A note at the bottom of the newly revised statement says: “Edits have been made to ensure this press release accurately reflects the government’s allegations in the affidavit in support of the domain seizures.”

The Justice Department said on Friday it made a correction to the news release because the August 26 release “described all agencies as victims whereas the government’s affidavit made clear that all were targeted but only some were compromised”.

The distinction matters because it narrows the scope of confirmed breaches.

The Justice Department has accused Chinese actors of a years-long cyber-espionage campaign against US government agencies, defence contractors and other sensitive targets.

According to an affidavit from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released alongside the original statement, the hackers have “targeted” US federal networks since at least 2018.

Those targets include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy (DOE), the Department of Justice, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US Senate.

A footnote in the affidavit said that the FBI investigated the targeting of NASA and found that the attempted breach of NASA was unsuccessful due to the agency’s patching of targeted software.

The affidavit alleges that in September 2024, the hackers carried out “computer intrusions” at three “DOE National Laboratories, NIH, an HHS agency, and a US security device manufacturer”. It referred to the entities as “victims”.

A separate joint cybersecurity advisory issued by the FBI, National Security Agency and US Cyber Command’s Cyber National Mission Force, published on Wednesday, listed successful data thefts from unnamed defence contractors, financial institutions and universities in May 2024.

It also noted unsuccessful attempts to access the networks for the US Senate and a hospital in March 2026.

Messages seeking clarification from the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency were not immediately returned on Friday.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters news agency on Friday.

In response to Wednesday’s announcement, an embassy spokesperson said the US uses cybersecurity to “smear or discredit China”.

It added that China “opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security and using it as a pretext to impose discriminatory restrictions on Chinese companies and will firmly safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies”.

title: Right-wing commentator Milo Yiannopoulos detained by ICE
excerpt:
Yiannopoulos seen holding a news conference in 2017

British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is awaiting deportati...
body_text:
Yiannopoulos seen holding a news conference in 2017

British right-wing political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos has been detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and is awaiting deportation.

Yiannopoulos, 41, a former editor of Breitbart News and onetime political aide to rapper Kanye West, appears to be held in Louisiana, according to ICE's inmate registry.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said he "was issued a final order of removal by an Immigration Judge on July 22, after failing to show up for his immigration hearing", and will remain in custody pending deportation.

The self-styled provocateur has called himself the "most fabulous supervillain on the internet". His critics call him a purveyor of hate speech.

Yiannopoulos, who grew up in Kent in the south of England, was arrested on 27 August after arriving at the airport in New Orleans.

He flew into the US in May 2019 and "chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation's laws", said DHS.

The DHS statement referred to him as "an illegal alien from the United Kingdom".

The BBC has asked the British embassy in Washington for comment. Yiannopoulos did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

"Being in detention is a choice," the DHS statement continued, calling on migrants who are in the US illegally to "self-deport now".

Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Donald Trump during the 2016 election, headlining an event that year called Gays for Trump during the Republican National Convention.

Yiannopoulos has become a critic of Trump, but still voices support for the Republican president's agenda. He posted in March this year on X that Trump "has lost his way, bought off by foreign interests".

Yiannopoulos has courted controversy with his comments on transgender people, Muslims, Black Lives Matter, feminists and gay people, even though he himself identified as gay. He now calls himself an "ex-gay".

In 2020, he assisted Kanye West in the rapper's bid to become president. He also worked for Marjorie Taylor Greene, a former Republican congresswoman who fell out with Trump and became a fierce critic before resigning from office.

He has written columns titled "Birth Control Makes Women Unattractive and Crazy" and "Would You Rather Your Child Had Feminism or Cancer?"

He has also cheered on ICE raids, writing on X last year: "Total legal immunity for ICE agents when they're on duty."

He posted in 2025: "We have got to deport millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters."

Yiannopoulos also advocated on social media for "on the spot deportation for anyone who can't prove they are in the US legally".

Laura Loomer, a far-right commentator and Trump ally who has feuded with Yiannopoulos, took credit for his arrest by ICE.

She posted on X on Friday night that his flight back to the UK had already departed.

"This subversive foreign agent is already out of the United States and DHS tells me he's NEVER allowed to come back to the United States ever again," she said.

In 2017, he was uninvited from speaking at CPAC, a US conservative conference that also hosted Trump, after footage emerged of Yiannopoulos appearing to condone paedophilia. He also later apologised and resigned from Breitbart.

He denied the allegations, and said he had been speaking about his own experiences as a child.

Yiannopoulos was once regularly linked with the alt-right, a disparate group that is outspoken against political correctness and feminism and which includes neo-Nazis and white supremacists.

He has said he does not consider himself part of the alt-right, although he has called it "energising and exciting".

Yiannopoulos event prompts violent protests

title: Woman allegedly ejected from roller coaster, suffers serious injuries after dragged along track: reports
excerpt:
A rider makes a split-second grab when another rider’s sneaker comes flying toward him aboard Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia as the roller coaster reaches roughly 70 mph.

A 60-year-old woman suffe...
body_text:
A rider makes a split-second grab when another rider’s sneaker comes flying toward him aboard Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia as the roller coaster reaches roughly 70 mph.

A 60-year-old woman suffered a broken rib, collapsed lung, a traumatic brain injury and a dislocated shoulder that required surgery after she was allegedly ejected from her seat on a Colorado roller coaster and dragged, according to reports and a law firm representing her.

Nicki Parker, of Texas, was thrown from her seat and dragged for 20 to 30 seconds after she remained strapped into her seat belt as the Rocky Mountain Coaster at Copper Mountain Resort kept going, FOX 31 Denver reported, citing her attorney.

"It was actually wrapped around her and pulled her and she was dragged along the track as it went down," Trent Ongert with Bloch Ongert Injury Law told the news station.

MONTANA BOY KILLED AFTER BEING FLUNG FROM CARNIVAL RIDE OPERATING WITH MISSING RESTRAINTS, LAWSUIT ALLEGES

A view of the Rocky Mountain Coaster at Copper Mountain Resort in Colorado. (Google Maps)

Ongert said Parker’s husband, who was riding behind her at the time, attempted to help her.

"She was lying on the track. He then had to get her out because there was nobody, no way to get to her," he explained. "They’re about 15 to 20 feet off the ground."

Parker remains hospitalized, Ongert said.

A sign posted along the ride says that the "cart will stop and beep" if the seat belt is disconnected.

COLLEGE GRAD REPORTEDLY DIES IN SIX FLAGS ROLLER COASTER INCIDENT AS FAMILY SUES THEME PARK

Copper Mountain Resort in Frisco, Colo. (Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post, File)

Colorado’s Division of Oil and Public Safety's Amusement Rides and Devices Program is investigating the incident.

"We can confirm our Division of Oil & Public Safety is investigating an incident that happened on Copper Mountain's Rocky Mountain Coaster on Monday, August 17, 2026," the agency told Fox News Digital. "One rider was injured in the incident. The Rocky Mountain Coaster is currently closed while the investigation continues. OPS has also told the manufacturer that they need to publish a safety bulletin and share it with all impacted operators.

"A similar ride operating at the Purgatory Resort is also closed pending the outcome of the investigation. Documentation involving the incident will not be made public until the investigation is complete."

JURY AWARDS TEENS $550K AFTER OREGON AMUSEMENT PARK RIDE LEFT THEM HANGING UPSIDE DOWN: REPORT

The section of Rocky Mountain Coaster alpine track at Copper Mountain in Colorado. (KDVR)

The roller coaster, which is 5,800 feet long and bills itself as the "2nd longest alpine coaster in North America," remains closed, according to its website.

"Our thoughts are with the guest, and we wish them a speedy recovery," the resort said in a press release sent to local outlets.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the agency, the resort and Ongert for comment.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: How 'Book Queen' Dolly Parton inspired millions of children with gift of reading
excerpt:
Dolly Parton first launched Imagination Library in her home county in Tennessee

One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".

Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted...
body_text:
Dolly Parton first launched Imagination Library in her home county in Tennessee

One child in Denver called her "The Book Queen".

Across the globe in Australia, a toddler with speech delays delighted her family with her first word - "orange" - after she and her twin sister received a free book in the post about colours. It came from Imagination Library, the literacy programme begun by late global superstar Dolly Parton.

Parton, who died this week aged 80, launched the philanthropic effort in 1995 to honour her father - whose difficult Appalachian upbringing never allowed him to finish school or learn to read and write.

"He was the smartest man I have ever known, but I know in my heart his inability to read probably kept him from fulfilling all of his dreams," wrote Parton in an open letter on Imagination Library's website.

"Inspiring kids to love to read became my mission."

London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe signed her daughter up for the scheme when she was three months old

Imagination Library sends one free book a month to children from birth to age five. It first launched in Tennessee's Sevier County, where Parton grew up, before expanding across the US in 2000. The programme, which partners with local organisations, launched in Canada in 2006, the UK the following year, then Australia in 2013 and Ireland in 2019.

By 2025, as Imagination Library celebrated its 30th anniversary, it had distributed more than 300m books - equating to one book mailed every 78 seconds, according to the organisation.

And for the families in receipt of the storybooks, the impact has been invaluable.

Tennessee governor plans to name Nashville airport after Dolly Parton

"It just blows my mind that it's readily available for every family that lives in my borough," said London mother-of-two Harriet Anscombe, whose four-year-old daughter has been receiving Imagination Library books since she was three months old.

The free books helped Anscombe establish a reading-focused nighttime routine.

"I think that, if I didn't get those books, maybe I wouldn't have started doing bedtime stories till she was two - but because we were getting them so early, it embedded story time into our routine from when she was just a couple of months old," Anscombe said. "She probably doesn't remember a time when we weren't reading stories."

Colorado mother Ciara Fernandez Faber's son called Parton 'the Book Queen'

Imagination Library became part of the family routine for Ciara Fernandez Faber, too, after she signed up her son about eight years ago in Colorado. His favourite book for years was one written by Parton herself: I Am A Rainbow.

"We read it almost every night, and I never got tired of reading it to him," said Faber, 42.

"It's a book about different emotions, and so we would act out the different emotions, the different faces," she said. "At the back of the book, there's a little excerpt by Dolly talking about how everybody has a rainbow of feelings, and we would read that - and he would always point to her picture and say, 'There's the Book Queen.'"

Families like Faber's repeatedly remarked on how well curated the books were - detailing how topics helped their children not just with reading, but also with social and emotional development.

"There were themes that were addressed in a lot of the books that would have really helped us navigate issues,"  said Helen Cashell, of Dublin, Ireland.

She signed up both of her children, now aged seven and five, for the scheme. "Whether it was same-sex families or just different types of families, things about bravery, courage, bullying, things about different identities."

Fernandez Faber's son, Aster, reads a book to his younger sister, Maya, in Colorado

Author Selina Brown, whose book My Rice Is Best was selected for distribution through Imagination Library, noted how the plotline features a black protagonist.

The programme also helps promote authors like herself; because of the selection, it "means 14,000 copies of my book have been sent to children in the UK".

"To choose between gas, electric, food or a book, you're going to choose a core need -  but with the Dolly Parton Imagination Library, you don't have to do that," she said.

In inner-city Sydney, Australia, first-time mum Paige Stewart was astounded as she watched her children's progress with the programme.

Her twin girls, now four, "had a speech delay and some learning difficulties" - but Stewart noticed a change after just the second book.

"Not only did they learn their colours from that book…  it kind of set the tone for them speaking and their joy for books."

She's become a vocal advocate for the programme, telling others: "It's so helpful, honestly."

In Dublin, Ireland, Helen Cashell's two children read books atop a pile of other titles they received in the post through Parton's Imagination Library

Alabama grandmother Kristina Hadley also promotes the programme to friends and family - even incorporating Imagination Library into baby gifts.

"I'll pull up the Imagination books website, and I'll print that, and I'll put it in a picture frame, and I'll get little newborn books and stuff like that, and I'll put it with that for like a suggestion for new mothers," said Hadley, 53.

She signed up her nearly three-year-old granddaughter, Eillie Elaine, "before she was actually born". Now the child has her own bookshelf in their shared household - "and one whole shelf is for her Dolly books".

"She likes to go to go to the mailbox, and she's like, 'Ms Dolly! Ms Dolly!' and I'm like, 'Well, let's go see if Ms Dolly sent you a book!'"

A lifelong Parton fan, Hadley chokes up while detailing how she was at work when a friend texted to say the singer had died.

Imagination Library, she says, "is going to keep her memory going with the younger generation, and I hope and I pray that this is something that goes on for years and years and years."

Children's author Selina Brown saw 14,000 copies of her book sent to kids in the UK

It's a legacy that Parton built quietly in the background as she presided over pop culture for more than six decades.

"The biggest thing that I like is the fact that she didn't do anything for recognition," said Geoff Blacklin, 67, of Manitoba, Canada.

He and his wife signed up their grandchildren for Imagination Library after a local doctor brought the programme to their region.

"She gave families more than books,"  Blacklin said. "She gave children a love of reading, precious moments with loved ones, and opportunities to learn and dream."

Such family stories and gratitude would undoubtedly have been music to Parton's ears; the expansion of the programme was truly a realisation of her own dream.

"In the beginning, my hope was simply to inspire the children in my home county, but here we are today with a worldwide programme that gives a book a month to well over 3 million children," she wrote on the Imagination Library site - also taking care to thank the partners "who have embraced my dream and made it their own".

At the centre of it, always, was her love for children - and her love for her father.

"Before he passed away, my Daddy told me the Imagination Library was probably the most important thing I had ever done," Parton wrote.

"I can't tell you how much that meant to me, because I created the Imagination Library as a tribute to my Daddy."

Dolly Parton was the one thing most Americans could agree on

Heart, hope and a steely determination: Dolly Parton's musical legacy

'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton

title: Landlady to 9/11 hijackers reveals their links to alleged Saudi spy
excerpt:
Holly Ratchford has decided to speak out publicly for the first time

Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accuse...
body_text:
Holly Ratchford has decided to speak out publicly for the first time

Holly Ratchford still cannot believe that the man who moved into the residential complex she once managed would go on to be accused of involvement in the darkest day in recent US history.

"It's almost impossible for me to wrap my head around who he said he was, and who he really is. I still struggle with that," she tells the BBC.

The man, Omar al-Bayoumi - a Saudi in his early 40s - moved to the complex in San Diego, California, with his family in September 1999.

The new resident at number 152 Parkwood Apartments quickly became a regular at Ratchford's pool parties. "He was always so bubbly and smiling," she recalls, "and just very, very friendly."

A few months later, Bayoumi would introduce Ratchford to two apparently unassuming, "polite" men, who would also become her neighbours.

The pair would become infamous for hijacking American Airlines flight 77, and crashing it into the Pentagon, in the 9/11 attacks.

Ratchford has been haunted by her connection to these three men for the past 25 years. She feels she was taken in by Bayoumi from the start.

"Whenever I had parties he would come and be a part of the activities," she recalls, adding that his family would invite her in for food.

But Bayoumi, the one-time resident of 152 Parkwood, is now at the centre of the $1 trillion (£733bn) lawsuit brought against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by several thousand families of victims and as well as survivors of 9/11.

On 11 September 2001, four passenger aircraft were hijacked by 19 members of the Islamist extremist network, al-Qaeda. In addition to the crash at the Pentagon - the US military's headquarters near Washington DC - two planes were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York, causing both buildings to collapse. A fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania, following resistance from passengers on board.

In all, almost 3,000 people were killed, including about 300 firefighters and other emergency workers at the World Trade Center.

The aftermath of the attack on the Pentagon on 9/11

Bayoumi is alleged to have facilitated the 9/11 plot through the support he provided for the first two hijackers to arrive in the US - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - who lived at Parkwood for several months prior to the attacks.

The federal judge in the 9/11 families' lawsuit in New York found a year ago that the evidence created "a reasonable inference" that Bayoumi and a Saudi diplomat based in the US had been "co-ordinating with the Saudi government when providing assistance to the hijackers".

The judge's ruling has allowed the families' case to move forward. Saudi Arabia is appealing it and, together with Bayoumi, has always denied the allegations.

Ever since the attacks, Bayoumi has been the subject of reporting and speculation.

Ratchford - who saw him interacting with the hijackers and witnessed him providing a crucial act of support for them - has given a sealed declaration to the New York court.

But she has never spoken publicly about what she saw.

Ratchford was property manager of Parkwood Apartments in the late 1990s

After unwittingly becoming embroiled in the investigation into what the US government has described as "the most egregious criminal act on American soil in modern history", she moved about as far from humanity as you can get in the United States.

I tracked her down to the high desert in the western US - rattlesnake country. She told me she avoided the news, and definitely did not speak to journalists. But, to my surprise, she agreed to talk.

Her interview with me casts doubt on the version of events Bayoumi has told police, the FBI and the New York court, and features in the BBC Radio 4 podcast, Intrigue: A 9/11 Story, and an upcoming BBC Panorama, 9/11: The Saudi Connection.

Twenty-five years on from the deadliest terror attack in history, Jane McMullen asks why thousands of grieving families are still fighting for answers.

In early 1999, Ratchford landed on her feet. Life before then had been untethered - she had moved around, been married, pregnant and divorced before she was 21. But now, aged 27, she had a job she loved and a home.

As the new property manager of Parkwood Apartments, a squat complex of 175 low-rise apartments and townhouses in the San Diego suburbs, she says she excelled. Properties were never empty for long. But it was not the paperwork, nor the healthy pay check, that made the job a dream, it was the people.

Ratchford not only worked at Parkwood, she lived there too. Her clients were also her neighbours. And many were more than that - she says they became her friends.

"I always told my staff: 'You make them feel like this is their home, and they'll stay,'" she recalls.

As Ratchford made her mark at Parkwood, she was happy and secure in the world she had built - a world in which she knew everyone and everything.

Then, things fell apart in a dramatic and unexpected way.

The Parkview Apartments complex, seen here today, in the San Diego suburbs

Omar al-Bayoumi moved into Parkwood claiming to be a mature student.

"I knew he was going to school. I'm not sure, other than that, what he did," Ratchford says.

More than two decades later, declassified FBI documents and court filings would reveal that Bayoumi's studies had, in effect, come to a halt in 1998. He was spending much more time organising religious activities in the Muslim community, which he often videotaped.

His constant filming, and his inquiring questions, aroused suspicions.

"It was a general consensus of people in the San Diego Muslim community that Bayoumi was an operative of the Saudi intelligence service," Richard Lambert, who led the city's FBI office investigation after 9/11, tells me.

But it was not Ratchford's business to pry. What mattered to her was whether he could pay the rent. And he could.

The FBI would later discover he was being paid about $90,000 (£55,600 at the time) a year.

Home videos show Bayoumi visiting Las Vegas and SeaWorld, and playing poolside with family

Bayoumi presented himself as an ordinary family man.

The Bayoumi who Ratchford saw was captured on his never-before-broadcast home movies - throwing a ball around with his family by the Parkwood pool, laughing when it drifted into the water.

Another video reveals him on an excursion to Las Vegas with his family. Wearing a floral shirt, he points out the rollercoaster by the New York, New York hotel casino.

"I bought into everything that he told me. I really thought that's how he was," Ratchford says.

But that version of Bayoumi is at odds with the man who emerges from other videos.

In summer 1999, Bayoumi filmed the United States Capitol in Washington DC from different angles, noting a "plan", and turning the camera on himself to deliver a reporter-style commentary.

The 9/11 families' lawyers allege he was surveilling the building as a potential target for the attacks. The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia maintains it is a tourist video.

In his August 2025 judgement, the New York judge found that "all the Court can conclude" from the video is that Bayoumi "visited Washington DC and that he filmed the city".

Bayoumi noted a "plan" while filming outside the Capitol

On 3 February 2000, Bayoumi brought two young men into Ratchford's San Diego rental office. In an obvious hurry, she says, he perched on the filing cabinet as he told her that the two men were from his mosque and were staying with him while they looked for a place to rent.

"There was absolutely nothing unusual about them. They were nice, they were polite," she recalls.

The two men spoke no English, but Bayoumi took charge. Ratchford says he asked her what the two men would need to show in order to qualify for a Parkwood apartment.

"They didn't meet the income criteria at all, or the bank account. They had none of that," she tells me.

But the two men did have several thousand dollars in cash. Bank records show that, the following day, Bayoumi took them to the nearest bank and helped them open an account.

Back at Ratchford's office on the third day, he figured a way around the problematic income criterion. He would co-sign their lease - becoming the legal guarantor for their apartment.

The rental agreement shows Bayoumi's multiple signatures. He was their guarantor, their friend, their emergency contact, and his Parkwood home was listed as their current address.

Without further delay, the two men moved into number 150, a one-bed apartment just a few doors down from Bayoumi's poolside townhouse.

The two men Bayoumi was assuming legal responsibility for - Nawaf al-Hazmi and Khalid al-Mihdhar - would become 9/11 hijackers.

Holly saw the pair repeatedly in the following few months.

"I would have cookies and tea with them. It wasn't like they were just someone that came into the office and rented from us," she says.

Hazmi and Mihdhar stayed in their apartment until the end of May that year, and then moved out. Ratchford thought no more about it.

Sixteen months later, as America reeled in shock and grief in the days following the 9/11 attacks, she says a woman called asking her for a rental reference for them. Without thinking, she rattled off their details.

But the woman was not a property agent - she was a reporter.

Her next question shook Ratchford: "Did you know that they were two of the terrorists that flew their plane into the Pentagon?"

Bayoumi was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch

On 14 September 2001, two special agents interviewed Ratchford in her Parkwood office.

She gave them Bayoumi's guarantor form, triggering an investigation into the man they would come to see as the main facilitator of the two hijackers' lives in San Diego.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI and working as a consultant to the 9/11 lawsuit families, says "as we began to identify the hijackers' associates, what became clear is that there was a network headed up by Omar al-Bayoumi".

The FBI found that Bayoumi's contacts had helped Hazmi and Mihdhar obtain California driver's licences, apply to flight schools, receive Middle Eastern wire transfers, and even arrange dental treatment.

The FBI agents wanted to interview Bayoumi. They traced him more than 5,000 miles (8,000km) to the UK, to Birmingham, where he had moved just before 9/11.

On 21 September 2001, he was arrested by the Metropolitan Police's anti-terror branch and detectives began questioning him.

Seeming unflustered, and at times indignant, Bayoumi initially denied knowing any of the hijackers.

Richard Lambert, now retired from the FBI, says Bayoumi headed up a network that involved the hijackers

He said he had often helped people find accommodation but, when detectives pressed him, said he could not remember the names of anyone for whom he had guaranteed an apartment.

A day later, he said he remembered helping two individuals, "Nawaf" and "Khalid" - the first names of Hazmi and Mihdhar.

He admitted they were the only two people to whom he had given this level of support.

Bayoumi claimed he had met the pair in Los Angeles, after briefly overhearing them speaking Arabic in a restaurant. He said he had told them that if they ever went to San Diego, he could help them.

The next day, he told the British detectives, the men had shown up at his local mosque in San Diego saying they needed a place to live. He had then driven them back to Parkwood to see Ratchford about finding them an apartment.

After Hazmi and Mihdhar had moved in, Bayoumi said he had avoided them. He said he had left town, and that when he returned, he found they had moved on.

In his account, Bayoumi's association with the future hijackers was fleeting. But his story does not match Ratchford's version of events.

Ratchford refutes Bayoumi's claim that his interactions with the hijackers were fleeting

"I know that's what he said, and I know that's bullshit," she says.

Before he brought the hijackers to her office, Ratchford says Bayoumi had asked her several times about finding an apartment for two people.

"I would tell him what would be available and he'd be like, 'oh no, no, I want that one'," she says. "He wanted something near him, and he was hoping for the least expensive place."

She also contradicts Bayoumi's claim that he hardly saw the hijackers after he secured their apartment, explaining that she had seen them together over the weeks that followed. On one occasion, the three of them had come to her office for tea and cookies.

"It's not like he just found them an apartment and never talked to them again," she says, adding that the three men "were definitely friendly".

Ratchford also told the FBI that when the hijackers had fallen behind with paying their rent, Bayoumi had paid it.

The Met Police held Bayoumi for seven days - the maximum at the time. The US Department of Justice (DOJ) decided not to extradite him to face charges.

On 28 September 2001, Bayoumi was released.

Bayoumi has never been prosecuted but the 9/11 families have pursued him through the courts

The FBI continued to build a case against him, however.

San Diego agents discovered that two companies linked to the Saudi Ministry of Defence were providing Bayoumi with his $90,000 pay, but that he never went to work and accrued "outrageous" expenses.

His pay more than doubled just after the two hijackers' arrival in San Diego, agents found, and fell again after they left the US west coast.

Meanwhile, agents from the New York FBI office combed through a trove of documents received from the Met Police, following the search of Bayoumi's properties in Birmingham, the BBC has learned.

The FBI uncovered letters to a Saudi government-linked charity with direct ties to al-Qaeda, materials which they assessed could "demonstrate Omar al-Bayoumi's anti-American sentiments and beliefs", and writings by Bayoumi himself which they determined "can be interpreted as jihadist".

But none of this led to an indictment or prosecution.

The DOJ told the BBC it was unable to comment on matters and decisions from 25 years ago, involving staff who no longer worked there.

9/11: What happened and how many people died in September 11 attacks?

Bayoumi left the UK for Saudi Arabia in August 2002.

Two years later, he was, in effect, cleared when the US's 9/11 Commission - the independent inquiry into the attacks - concluded he was "obliging and gregarious" and "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists". The FBI had not shown the Commission all the evidence it had gathered - and declined to comment when the BBC asked about this.

Meanwhile, the 9/11 families had started their attempts to pursue him through the courts, adding him as a defendant to their $1tn suit against various individuals, companies and governments for allegedly supporting al-Qaeda.

For years, the families campaigned for the FBI's investigation to be declassified. The wait was agonisingly slow, but since 2018 tens of thousands of pages of documents have been released to the New York court and via a presidential order signed by Joe Biden - including the FBI's interviews with Holly Ratchford.

In August last year, having considered the entire body of evidence, the judge in the 9/11 families' legal case said the evidence did not support the conclusion that Bayoumi had been "just an innocent participant".

Judge George B Daniels also noted later in his judgement that there was "a reasonable inference that all the apartment-related assistance he [Bayoumi] provided for the hijackers was not just acts of a good Samaritan, but rather that he was following" instructions from the Saudi government.

Saudi Arabia denies any involvement in 9/11 and has consistently argued that Omar al-Bayoumi was not a Saudi agent and did not have any involvement or foreknowledge of the attacks. It maintains that, under US law, it has sovereign immunity - official exemption of a ruler or state from certain types of civil suit and criminal prosecution - and that the case should be struck out.

The case is now with the US Court of Appeal, which will hear oral arguments in October.

Ratchford now lives in an isolated area in the west of the US

9/11 was a catastrophe that wrought personal trauma on tens of thousands of people - the families of the victims, the survivors, first responders and witnesses.

For Holly Ratchford, all the certainties and securities of her years at Parkwood came to an abrupt end.

"I know a lot of peoples' lives changed immediately during 9/11. For me, within a week or two, my life, my ideals, my beliefs, everything changed so quickly. It was like a flip of a switch," she says.

"I felt so stupid. I trusted and I cared about people that did bad things. I don't ever want to be as blindsided as I was by them not being who they said they were."

Soon after 9/11, Ratchford quit Parkwood, property management, and the big city.

She moved first to the beach, then to a reservation, and later, to the middle of nowhere - all in an effort to escape the feeling she was being tricked.

Ratchford kept to herself, she tells me, interacting only with people she absolutely trusted.

"9/11 made me afraid of people," she says.

"Now I just prefer to be away from people that might be lying about who they are. You can't keep a secret when you live in a small town and that makes me feel more safe. I like being in a place where I can trust people."

But even as she has sought to escape further and further from the outside world, she is haunted by questions about what happened at Parkwood.

"Part of me wonders if there's something I could have done if I was more strict," she says.

title: Tarik Skubal gets emotional during highly anticipated return to Detroit after blockbuster trade
excerpt:
Dakich calls out Michal Alter's ignorance.

Earlier this month, the Los Angeles Dodgers pulled off a blockbuster trade with the Detroit Tigers that brought aboard two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal...
body_text:
Dakich calls out Michal Alter's ignorance.

Earlier this month, the Los Angeles Dodgers pulled off a blockbuster trade with the Detroit Tigers that brought aboard two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Now, just weeks later, the Dodgers rolled into Motor City, and guess who got the start?

TARIK SKUBAL SAYS HE WAS EMOTIONAL LEAVING DETROIT TIGERS FOR LA DODGERS, WOULD LOVE TO RETURN: 'I'M CRYING'

Outfielder Zyhir Hope and right-handed pitchers Brady Smith and River Ryan went the other way in the deal.

Skubal's return to Detroit came at an interesting time as the NL West leaders came into the evening fresh off of three-straight losses to the Atlanta Braves.

So, despite all of the emotions, Skubal had some important work to do on the hill.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Dodgers pitcher Tarik Skubal gets emotional during a video tribute ahead of his return to Comerica Park to face the Detroit Tigers. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

Those emotions briefly got the best of him when the Tigers played a tribute video on the big screen. The right-hander got a little misty-eyed as fans gave him a standing ovation.

Detroit's Drew Anderson went through the first half-inning with a pair of strikeouts early, and with that it was time for Skubal to take the mound at Comerica Park in a Dodgers uniform.

A mix of boos and cheers as he walked out onto the field.

However, before he threw his first pitch, there was a light-hearted moment when Skubal's PitchCom wasn't working right.

Tarik Skubal gave up an early double, but managed to get out of the first inning against the Tigers unscathed. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images)

The Tigers' second baseman, Gleyber Torres, was the first former teammate Skubal had to face, and it didn't go particularly well as he sent a pitch deep to center field over Dodger Alek Thomas' head for a double.

However, after that, he notched a pair of strikeouts and got out of the inning without allowing a run.

title: US judge rejects Trump’s bid to switch hush-money case to federal court
excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump has once again lost a bid to transfer his criminal hush-money case from state to federal court, in a bid to have his felony conviction dropped.

On Friday, Judge A...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump has once again lost a bid to transfer his criminal hush-money case from state to federal court, in a bid to have his felony conviction dropped.

On Friday, Judge Alvin Hellerstein declined Trump’s petition for a third time, ruling that the president’s arguments were “neither new nor legally sufficient”.

Trump became the first US president to be convicted of a crime in 2024, when a New York City jury found him guilty of 34 counts of falsifying business records.

Prosecutors had argued that Trump attempted to conceal hush-money payments to the adult film star Stormy Daniels, to avoid negative attention during his 2016 presidential bid.

Trump, however, has maintained that his conviction should be tossed, given a 2024 Supreme Court decision expanding presidential immunity. But Hellerstein once again rejected that argument.

“Paying hush money to an adult film star or engaging in a cover-up of an embarrassment are not subsumed in presidential immunity,” Hellerstein wrote.

Trump’s lawyers have already announced they would appeal, denouncing Hellerstein’s judgement as “baseless and lawless”.

“President Trump will be filing a powerful appeal, and will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn,” a statement from Trump’s team said.

The case centres on a $130,000 payment Trump allegedly made through his fixer, Michael Cohen, to buy Daniels’s silence, after she claimed she had an affair with the Republican leader while he was married. Trump has denied any sexual liaison with Daniels.

Falsifying business records in New York is normally a misdemeanour, but it can be charged as a felony when committed in service of another crime. In the hush-money case, prosecutors claimed Trump had sought to unlawfully influence the 2016 election, which he ultimately won.

The New York indictment was one of four Trump faced in 2023, between his two terms as president.

The other indictments concerned allegations that Trump illegally withheld classified documents and attempted to undermine the 2020 elections, which he lost. Those cases were ultimately dropped after Trump won re-election in 2024.

Of the four indictments, only the New York case reached trial. While the felony convictions made Trump eligible for incarceration or a fine, Judge Juan Merchan ultimately sentenced the Republican leader to an unconditional discharge.

That meant he would face no jail time, nor a financial penalty, but the convictions would remain on his records. The sentencing came on January 10, 2025, just days before Trump’s second inauguration.

Trump has appealed his conviction in the years since the trial, and simultaneously has attempted to move the case to federal court, where he likewise hopes he can toss the charges.

As part of his appeal, Trump’s legal team has cited a July 2024 ruling from the Supreme Court, expanding the concept of presidential immunity.

Previously, presidents were shielded from prosecution for actions taken within their constitutional mandate. The 2024 decision broadened that scope to give presidents “presumptive immunity” for anything that could be considered an “official act”, an undefined concept.

Trump’s lawyers argued that, since the hush-money case presented evidence from his first term as president, it falls under that immunity.

Hellerstein has previously rejected that argument. In November, however, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals ordered Hellerstein to reconsider the case in light of the Supreme Court’s decision.

The appeals court, however, did not instruct Hellerstein how he should rule. In Friday’s decision, Hellerstein rejected implications from the Trump team that he would simply certify the appeals court ruling.

“Federal district courts are not certifying clerks,” the judge wrote.

Hellerstein also addressed the Supreme Court’s decision, ruling that Trump’s actions with regard to Daniels were not “official acts” of the presidency, even if some were taken while he was in office.

“There is no way that discussions regarding hush money payments to cover up the President’s relations with Stormy Daniels could be an official act. An affair, or a cover-up of an affair, is not within the ‘outer perimeter’ of the President’s official responsibilities,” Hellerstein wrote.

title: Trump border wall construction kicks off in Arizona amid clash with Native American tribe
excerpt: Aerial video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers in Texas before the vehicle was disabled and the occupants fled, with officials saying one suspect later carjacked a civilian at gunpo...
body_text:
Aerial video shows authorities pursuing suspected human smugglers in Texas before the vehicle was disabled and the occupants fled, with officials saying one suspect later carjacked a civilian at gunpoint. (@CBPCommissioner via X)

The Trump administration has started construction of a section of a border wall in Arizona despite objections from a Native American tribe.

The wall is part of a $46 billion effort to shore up the southern border with 30-foot steel bollard walls, vehicle barriers, and technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.

However, the Tohono O'odham Nation has said the construction will damage land sacred to the tribe, The Associated Press reported.

MULLIN TELLS CONGRESS PRIMARY BORDER WALL WILL BE DONE BY JUNE 2027, SECONDARY WALL BY SUMMER 2028

Contractors drill at a border wall pre-construction site in Arizona on Tuesday. The project is part of a Trump administration effort to shore up the southern border, which came amid opposition from the Tohono O'odham Nation, which said contractors are trespassing on tribal land. (Tohono O'odham Nation via AP)

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said the desert spanning the Tohono O’odham Nation, which sits on both sides of the border, is a major corridor for drug smuggling.

"The project will close one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border: remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity," said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott.

TRUMP TO SHRINK 2 UTAH NATIONAL MONUMENTS BY 90%

The tribe, which has 37,000 members, including many who live in Mexico, sued the federal government in June in an attempt to halt the project.

The lawsuit argued the construction would cause "significant devastation" on the reservation, including the destruction of mountain peaks sacred to the tribe.

TRUMP SCORES MAJOR IMMIGRATION VICTORY AS JUDGE CLEARS WAY TO END TPS PROTECTIONS FOR THOUSANDS OF SOMALIS

Contractors drill at a border wall pre-construction site in Arizona on Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026. (Tohono O'odham Nation via AP)

A federal judge rejected the argument, siding with the government and noting that the border wall would be built on a 60-foot-wide buffer zone of federally owned land called the Roosevelt Reservation.

"Defendants have not yet articulated plans to construct outside the Roosevelt Reservation," U.S. District Judge Richard Leon in Washington, D.C., wrote in his opinion.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION NAMES ROSARIO 'PETE' VASQUEZ TO SERVE AS NEXT US BORDER PATROL CHIEF

FILE - Illegal Mexican immigrants walk through the Sonoran Desert after illegally crossing the U.S.-Mexico border border on January 19, 2011 into the Tohono O'odham Nation, Arizona. The immigrants said they had wandered the desert lost for a week after crossing from Mexico into the vast Indian reservation at night. Exhausted, they requested the Border Patrol to pick them up and take them to the U.S.-Mexico border, from where they would return to their homes in the Mexican state of Sonora. They had come, they said, to reach Phoenix and find work in construction or landscaping. All said they had worked in Arizona before. (John Moore/Getty Images)

The tribe said the construction still constitutes trespassing, even if the project is contained to the Roosevelt Reservation. The tribe set up "No Trespassing" signs this week and said masked CBP agents set up a vehicle blockade to stop tribal police from removing the contractors.

"The contractors, who are on the Nation illegally, were accompanied by agents as they worked on three separate locations near the border with drill trucks to conduct soil sampling and other activities," tribal officials said in a statement.

The U.S.-Mexico border fence ends at the eastern edge of the Tohono O’odham Reservation near Sasabe, Arizona, U.S., May 10, 2022. (Reuters/Rebecca Noble)

The tribe said it was exploring other legal means to remove the contractors.

Fox News Digital has reached out to CBP and the Tohono O'odham Nation for comment.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Satellite images reveal scale of flood devastation in Nepal villages
excerpt:
Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood

New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered...
body_text:
Tracing the deadly path of the Nepal-Tibet flash flood

New satellite imagery has revealed the scale of the devastation along Nepal's Trishuli River caused by Wednesday's deadly flash flood, triggered by a glacier collapse.

Before-and-after images show how sections of the valley, where a torrent of floodwater and debris surged through, destroyed villages, bridges and hydroelectric power stations.

More than 550 people have been killed, Nepalese officials say, with hundreds more missing.

Among the worst-hit locations reviewed by BBC Verify was a key Nepal-Tibet border crossing, which was engulfed by a rush of floodwater and captured on camera.

The satellite imagery from US-based intelligence firm Vantor, shows the site has been almost entirely washed away. Shocking CCTV footage showed the moment as the deluge of water swept over buildings as people tried to escape.

Damage and mud can be seen more than 2.5km (1.5 miles) upstream, reaching 100m (330 ft) above the area it first hit.

A few miles further south is the village of Timure, which has now largely disappeared.

The walls of the valley at this point are steep, reaching up to 50m above the water line. The image shows most of the houses perched on this slope are now gone or covered in mud.

A further 10km (eight miles) downstream, where the Trishuli River winds through Syapru Besi, satellite imagery now shows the village covered by mud, rock and other debris. Houses and other structures have disappeared, including bridges and a hydroelectric power station.

One of the larger villages to be struck by the full force of the flood was Trishuli, where some of the earliest verified footage of the disaster emerged from.

A satellite image of the town and surrounding agricultural land, which is about 45km (28 miles) downstream from the border, show an entire neighbourhood has been essentially washed away.

Verified videos of the town show a bridge collapsing as the river surges forward. At the very same moment from ground level, footage filmed from inside a bus shows people crying out in distress and trying to flee as they see the water rushing down the river.

Other dramatic videos show people sheltering inside a house, peering over the edge of a balcony as they watch a torrent of floodwater wash away almost everything around them, knocking large metal debris and a vehicle toward the building.

Somehow the house remains intact and survivors can be seen in a second verified video standing surrounded by mud once the floodwater had receded.

Imagery from satellite provider Planet Labs released today has also provided a clearer view of the disaster's origins at the collapsed glacier, the moment of which has been captured on a verified drone video.

The satellite image shows an enormous chunk of the glacier has fallen away, carving an enormous path of rock and debris where water rushed through the valley.

At the base of the landslide, trees and other vegetation have been stripped at a height of more than 300m above the riverbed.

This destructive path continues westwards along with the swelled river, before heading southwards.

Satellite images also show the formation of a barrier lake at the base of the landslide's path, which Chinese authorities have warned poses a major risk of further flooding and has hampered rescue efforts.

Dr Argha Banerjee, a glaciologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, told BBC Verify that it was not possible determine from the images how stable the barrier was or how likely the lake was to drain suddenly.

But he said there was no significant increase in its surface area between Wednesday and Thursday, despite water continuing to flow into the lake.

Dr Banerjee said there was a visible drainage channel, which suggests some water was already escaping downstream, adding that the its volume was "not alarmingly large" and appeared to have stabilised.

The extent of the damage on the Tibetan side of the border remains unclear. It is a strictly controlled region which China annexed in the 1950s, where foreign media access is heavily restricted. BBC Verify has so far been unable find verifiable footage from the area.

The satellite imagery - which only provides an initial glimpse into the damage of the flood - has been published by Vantor as part of its Open Data Program to help aid authorities establish where best to focus their efforts to locate the missing, rescue survivors and recover the dead.

Additional reporting Shruti Menon, Merlyn Thomas and Alex Murray. Graphics by Mezut Ersoz.

title: Good Good Golf doesn't deserve to be canceled for their dumb ad in collaboration with Callaway
excerpt: Will Cain and Sage Steele expose the left's selective application of cancel culture standards after Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner's primary victory. Cain questions why past controversies like ...
body_text:
Will Cain and Sage Steele expose the left's selective application of cancel culture standards after Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner's primary victory. Cain questions why past controversies like Nazi tattoos and sexting scandals didn't hinder Platner's political movement, suggesting an agenda over principles. Steele highlights historical examples of perceived double standards in media.

Cancel culture is making a comeback, unfortunately.

In case you missed it, Good Good Golf has been dragged by the golf establishment for an advertisement they posted in collaboration with Callaway golf, which promoted the Quantum Max Driver with Good Good branding. The ad features many of Good Good's top personalities, including co-founder Garrett Clark, who is seen shoving a woman before she's able to get a hold of the driver in his bag. He stands over her as she lays on the ground and tells her not to touch his driver.

Reading this makes it sounds bad, and watching it is "cringe," as Clark stated, while apologizing in a lengthy Instagram post following the backlash. The advertisement was done and presented in poor taste and the public didn't receive it well. Even though it was meant to take inspiration from the hit horror movie "Obsession," as Clark stated in his instagram video, where a character becomes obsessed with another due to a magic spell, causing them to be insanely and violently overprotective, it was not perceived that way. Many viewers missed the point and it fell flat, to say the least. But, what has been done in the aftermath since the deleted post, is what is unjust and concerning to me.

NFL PUTS 'INSPIRE CHANGE' AND 'CHOOSE LOVE' ON FIELDS BUT NOT SO AGGRESSIVE ABOUT ITS DOMESTIC ABUSE ISSUES

Garrett Clark adjusts his hat while standing on the 15th green during the 2025 Tour Championship Creator Classic, presented by YouTube, before the TOUR Championship at East Lake Golf Club in Atlanta, Ga., on Aug. 20, 2025. (PGA TOUR)

This whole situation has turned into a way for companies to virtue signal about domestic violence and supporting women, though most, if not all of these companies have done nothing to protect women and girls as their sports and spaces have been invaded by males over the years. Clark, in a 9-minute long video said neither him, nor the company, support or meant to insinuate any form of domestic violence. It was clearly a skit, but retail companies and even the PGA Tour are actively cancelling the popular YouTube golf brand, making them the fall guy for an ad that Callaway is just as responsible for, in my opinion.

YOUTUBE GOLFER GRANT HORVAT IS SELLING KIDS GOLF CLUBS WITH AN ALARMINGLY HIGH PRICE TAG

Golf Galaxy, Dick's Sporting Goods, Target, and the PGA Superstore have pulled Good Good products from their shelves and online. Golf Channel cancelled the latest season of the reality show in collaboration with Good Good, "Big Break." Good Good announced Thursday the cancelation of their title sponsorship for the PGA Tour event, the Good Good Championship in Texas saying, "After thoughtful discussion with the PGA Tour and careful reflection, we have decided to step away as sponsor of the Tour event in Austin this Fall." Callaway also ended their partnership with the popular golf brand stating, "we have listened and reflected deeply on the hurt and disappointment caused by the video we reposted. We heard from individuals who shared personal experiences related to violence against women, and their stories were powerful reminders that this issue touches the lives of far too many people. Unequivocally, violence against women is unacceptable and should never be trivialized, normalized, or used as entertainment." Yes, violence and mistreatment of women should be called out and women and girls should be protected, but these decisions and statements are just pure, unadulterated corporate virtue signaling.

Dick's Sporting Goods will add Collectors Clubhouse areas to its House of Sports locations. (Photo by Marcin Golba/NurPhoto)

MARY CAIN'S BOOK AND NIKE'S TRANS-ATHLETE STUDY REVEAL THE SAME PATTERN OF CORPORATE HYPOCRISY

Has Callaway's merch been pulled from stores? Nope.

Has Callaway dealt with any reprecussions from the PGA Tour? Nope.

That is exactly what Good Good Golf CEO, Matt Kendrick called out early this morning in a post on X stating, "Interesting that @CallawayGolf asks us to make an ad then approves it then asks us to take the fall then drops us in a coordinated media blitz and covers it up by giving a million dollars away thinking everyone will be ok with it."

In other words, Good Good is the bad guy, and Callaway gets to virtue signal their way into receiving no backlash from the golf establishment and media because they're donating $1 million "to support organizations working to prevent violence against women, provide resources to survivors, and advance education and awareness efforts." Good grief. Get off your high horse, Callaway.

This is clear and obvious cancel culture.

Brad Dalke, Garrett Clark, and Sean Walsh, pose for a photo together, on the 10th tee box, during the 2025 Tour Championship Creator Classic, prior to TOUR Championship, at East Lake Golf Club, on August 20, 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Ben Jared/PGA TOUR via Getty Images) (Ben Jared/PGA TOUR via Getty Images)

PEREZ HILTON JOINS 'TOMI LAHREN IS FEARLESS' AND DECLARES CANCEL CULTURE IS NOW A SPORT

Cancel culture is an unjustified public shaming and social ostracism for a perceived wrong, mostly due to something liberals consider not politically correct under their ridiculous societal standards. It's not an actual wrong, worthy of relentless public shaming and corporate canceling.

When I told people publicly to avoid shopping and supporting Bud Light, Target, Ulta and others promoting transgenderism through kids clothing, "tuck-friendly" swimwear, a man pretending to be a woman telling women how to be women (Dylan Mulvaney), that is not cancel culture. That's an objective moral wrong. Companies promoting body mutilation through "gender affirming care", gender fluidity, and more nonsense, is worth boycotting.

FROM COLIN KAEPERNICK TO DYLAN MULVANEY, NIKE'S DECADE OF LEFT-WING ACTIVISM HAS FINALLY CAUGHT UP TO IT

The Bud Light boycott was the most successful boycott in recent history after they partnered with Mulvaney to celebrate "one year of womanhood." It was a justified boycott. Anyone comparing Bud Light to this poorly-acted, dumb advertisement, which was obviously presented in poor taste, is being dishonest.

Cancel culture was Twitter banning and suspending accounts like The Babylon Bee, myself, Charlie Kirk, and many others years ago, for calling former Assistant Secretary for Health under the Biden administration, Rachel Levine and swimmer Lia Thomas, men.

Dylan Mulvaney accepts the Streamy Award for Breakout Creator onstage at The 2023 Streamy Awards held at the Fairmont Century Plaza Hotel on Aug. 27, 2023 in Los Angeles, California. (Rich Polk/Penske Media via Getty Images)

DAN GAINOR: WE GOT TWITTER/X AS A PLATFORM 20 YEARS AGO AND GLOBAL CENSORS STILL HATE AND FEAR IT

Cancel Culture is Fanatics firing from hosting their live shows in 2021 because I went to the gym without a mask in Arizona, the day the Governor dropped the mask mandate.

What is being done to Good Good is cancel culture. It’s wrong.

Clark never actually shoved that woman, as he stated on Instagram. It was acting. Yes, poor acting and a very bad idea. I've stated online that I have no idea why they thought this way a good idea, especially in a culture ready and willing to overreact, but it was in no way a promotion or endorsement of domestic violence.

NIKE REMOVES RUNNING AD IN BOSTON FOR 'PACE SHAMING'

I can relate to this in a real way because I was an actor in a video for my Christian college's chapel program, where I played a version of the old Terry Tate: Office Linebacker Reebok commercial, where he tackled men and men throughout the office. I "tackled" and "shoved" men and women in the video. I even stood over a female chapel card monitor yelling at her for accepting a blank chapel attendance card from a student. It was clearly satire. It was a dumb, yet fun video. No women were harmed. No women were outraged. Thousands laughed when it was shown at a semester-end chapel. No one was canceled or was called to be canceled.

There have been many advertisements over the years with men tackling or shoving women. Betty White got trucked in a Snickers commercial playing football.

In an early 2000s commercial, Michelob Ultra portrayed a woman getting viciously tackled in a football game at a park. There was a clear understanding of satire and acting. It wasn't real. It wasn't a prescription for abusing women.

More than anything, there's a clear double standard at play with the way Callaway is being treated by the PGA Tour, Golf Channel, and retailers.

Callaway saw this dumb advertisement in collaboration with Good Good Golf, signed off on it, published it, and they are going through the situation unscathed.

A detailed view of a Callaway Chrome Tour X golf ball on a tee prior to the Hero Dubai Desert Classic at Emirates Golf Club on January 15, 2024 in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. (Photo by Richard Heathcote/Getty Images) (Richard Heathcote/Getty Images)

No, I'm not calling for Callaway to be canceled. Both should have just said the ad was dumb, apologized for how it was received, taking accountability for a lack of clear messaging, saying that it was a spin-off of Obessesion, and move on.

Instead, Good Good is faced with their products no longer in major retailers, pushed out of their title sponsorship for a PGA Tour event, and a public corporate shaming that is one of the worst in history. All because the PGA Tour and corporations want to make an example out of a group, so they can look morally superior. It's shameful.

Jon is a writer and content creator for OutKick

title: Thieves steal 600-diamond necklace from Vienna museum in broad daylight
excerpt:
Vienna police released CCTV images of the suspects

An international manhunt is under way for two men who stole a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds from a museum in Vienna after buying a ...
body_text:
Vienna police released CCTV images of the suspects

An international manhunt is under way for two men who stole a necklace decorated with more than 600 diamonds from a museum in Vienna after buying a ticket for the exhibition in which it was being displayed.

Police said the two suspects smashed a glass display case at the Vienna Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) on Thursday afternoon and grabbed the platinum and diamond necklace, which is believed to be worth more than $4m (£3m; €3.5m).

The necklace, which was designed for the former Egyptian royal family, was part of an exhibition on the jewellers Van Cleef & Arpels, due to run at MAK until September.

The theft is the latest in a series of spectacular heists of artefacts at European museums.

Vienna police released photos of the two suspects, who were unmasked, captured on security cameras. They are appealing for the public to come forward with information.

The police said in a statement that one of the perpetrators was also believed to have been carrying what was thought to be a real firearm.

After seizing the necklace, they fled "towards the Vienna Stadtpark" just south of the museum, they said.

The more than 200-carat necklace was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter to the future Shah of Iran

Lilli Hollein, MAK general director, said "the theft of a highly valuable piece of jewellery... has hit us hard".

She said in a statement that MAK had developed a security plan with Van Cleef & Arpels specifically for the exhibition, adding: "Security issues were taken very seriously and all security measures were carefully prepared."

Hollein said staff had reacted calmly and followed the established procedures when the "armed incident" occurred, and that no one had been injured.

She added that MAK had thoroughly reviewed its security measures ahead of the exhibition, "particularly in light of the incidents at major museums in recent years".

Also on Thursday was one of the most important troves of prehistoric jewellery and artefacts was stolen from a Spanish museum.

Four Renaissance paintings were stolen from a museum in Sicily earlier this month, while three paintings by Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse worth millions of euros were taken from a museum in Parma earlier in the year.

These heists came after the brazen daylight raid on the Louvre in Paris, in which a masked gang stole priceless jewels last October.

The exhibition, minus the stolen necklace, reopened later on Friday

The string of thefts have raised questions about the security of European cultural institutions.

Europol said museum thefts were "becoming increasingly aggressive, with a shift towards violent and forceful methods", adding this "may indicate the involvement of new criminal networks".

The necklace stolen in Vienna on Friday was designed for the former Egyptian royal family and was worn by Queen Nazli in 1939 for the marriage of her daughter Fawzia to the future Shah of Iran, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi.

Van Cleef & Arpels describes it as a "triumph of white jewellery". The diamonds on the necklace weigh in excess of 200 carats.

When it was auctioned a decade ago, it had an estimated worth of $3.6m-$4.6m.

Police dog units have been deployed in Vienna and the province of Lower Austria, while forensic experts are analysing evidence and CCTV footage.

Four 'extraordinary' Renaissance paintings stolen from Italian museum

Thieves steal Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse paintings in three-minute Italian heist

'Priceless' jewels stolen in raid on Louvre Museum in Paris

excerpt:

As Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., laughs off the excesses of what she now calls "Woke 1.0," it is worth rememb...
body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

As Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., laughs off the excesses of what she now calls "Woke 1.0," it is worth remembering just how bad censorship was under that politically correct cultural regime, and how it got so bad that Hollywood conservatives needed to form their own secret club.

In a recent podcast interview, actress Patricia Heaton, of ‘Everybody Loves Raymond’ fame, spilled the beans on Friends of Abe, a secret organization for conservatives and independents in the entertainment industry, which she helped form during the Obama administration.

Abe, in this case, references the first Republican president, Abraham Lincoln.

FILE - Patricia Heaton urged her "friends on the left" to reject violent political rhetoric following the White House Correspondents' Dinner shooting. Heaton allegedly participated in the Friends of Abe group. (Brian Stukes/Getty Images)

AOC SAYS ‘WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY,’ BUT DEMOCRATS STILL OWE VOTERS AN EXPLANATION

A small core group that included stars such as Gary Sinise and Kelsey Grammar, soon turned into a loose organization of thousands, with a New York City chapter that I joined somewhere around 2012, and which was an oasis in a Gotham arts scene that made Mao look like William F. Buckley, Jr.

As Heaton put it, "You could ask someone if they are a friend of Abe, or FOA, and if they said yeah, then you know there was another conservative or independent, or someone who is not a Democrat, that you could talk to without feeling like you were going to get in trouble at your job."

FILE - Actress Patricia Heaton described Friends of Abe as a safe place for conservatives. (Roy Rochlin / Getty)

KELSEY GRAMMER SUSPECTS HE 'MAY HAVE' LOST HOLLYWOOD ROLES DUE TO CONSERVATIVE VIEWS

It is hard to overstate just how dangerous expressing conservative ideas was 5 to 15 years ago in the entertainment industry. Take actor Gina Carano, who lost her role in a Disney TV show because she posted on social media that conservatives should not be treated as enemies.

In the New York theater scene at this time, in which many New York Friends of Abe toiled, to even question progressive shibboleths on the trans issue or, eventually, the evils of President Donald Trump, could garner a lifetime ban.

GINA CARANO SAYS DISNEY WENT QUIET AFTER SETTLEMENT AS SHE GEARS UP FOR ROUSEY FIGHT

A conservative in theater was so rare, that when I "came out" as a conservative, as host of a regular 10-minute series, and sparred with the Bowery Poetry Club's hyper liberal audience, people — including good friends of mine — assumed for years that I was doing a bit.

For many in the arts at that time, including on the technical side of things, being known as right wing could have real consequences — as direct as not getting a job, or as indirect as just not getting invited to professional events.

FILE - US actress Gina Carano arrives for the Disney+ world premiere of "The Mandalorian" at El Capitan Theatre in Hollywood on Nov. 13, 2019. (Nick Agro/AFP)

KEVIN SORBO BLASTS HOLLYWOOD 'BLACKLISTING' OF CONSERVATIVES AS 'SEVENTH GRADE MEAN GIRLS' CULTURE

What made Friends of Abe’s monthly meetups so special for us was just that we could talk freely, something that, prior to the emergence of wokeness, we all took for granted. None of us take it for granted anymore.

When we look at how few liberals say they are proud of our nation, and how many — like Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico — say the American flag is a "complicated symbol," can there be any doubt that the wholesale excising of conservative ideas from Hollywood played a role in that?

There was almost nobody in Hollywood writing rooms — save maybe for shows like South Park and a few others — defending the founding fathers, stressing how far race relations in America have come, or, God forbid, questioning the ability of men to transform themselves into women.

As meaningful and important as the fellowship that FOA provided was for its members, the fact that it was needed at all goes a long way to showing just how intolerant of conservative ideas the entertainment industry had become, and for many conservative Americans, how detached it was from their own realities.

STEPHEN COLBERT'S 'LATE SHOW' JOKES TARGETED CONSERVATIVES 87% OF TIME IN FINAL YEARS, STUDY SAYS

The mere fact that Heaton can talk about FOA today does show a real thawing from the censorious ice age we recently came through. Today, more celebrities are comfortable talking about conservative ideals, including their faith.

But, make no mistake, there is still a long way to go. Just because people aren’t being fired for tweets anymore, doesn’t mean that Hollywood isn’t still 95% progressive, and that its output won’t continue to reflect that.

Though I’m not in the industry anymore, I’m glad conservatives who still are don’t need to hide it so much anymore, and hope that their influence is soon felt on our screens and in our lives. Until then, and even after, I will remain a proud friend of Abe.

David Marcus is a columnist living in West Virginia and the author of "Charade: The COVID Lies That Crushed A Nation."

title: Trump’s agriculture secretary commits to ‘waiving red tape’ to allow ranchers to process and sell their own beef – live
