title: Fears for ‘gregarious’ local celebrity Sammy the elephant seal in Victorian bird flu hotspot
excerpt:
Seals and sea lions often communicate by touch and share spaces with wild birds, placing them at risk of infection from H5N1 virus

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our brea...
body_text:
Seals and sea lions often communicate by touch and share spaces with wild birds, placing them at risk of infection from H5N1 virus

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Since H5 bird flu arrived in Portland, Victoria, the situation has been “pretty grim” with many dead and suffering birds on the beach, and the dilemma of how to dispose of the carcasses, according to local resident Lynn Murrell.

But since the first confirmed case in a fur seal on Sunday at Beachport, South Australia – a two-hour trip over the border – people have been worried for their local “pet seal”, known as Sammy.

“He’s a great tourist attraction. The locals love him. So, we’d hate to see him get the flu,” Murrell, the president of the Southwest Environment Alliance, a coalition of local environment groups, said.

The male southern elephant seal had “kind of adopted the town”, frequenting the foreshore and port, and sometimes the community gardens. In recent weeks, the seal has been spotted near birds presumed to have died from H5N1.

Victoria’s first bird flu case was detected in the town, in the far south-west of the state, at the end of July. Since then, the area has become a hotspot, with 17 confirmed events in crested terns, magpies, silver gulls and ravens, according to the federal agriculture department, and many more suspected cases.

People were concerned about the carcasses, and the risk of the virus spreading as a result of scavengers eating them. Some have estimated 30 to 40 new sick and dying birds on the beach a day.

A spokesperson for Glenelg shire council said the situation was distressing for many in the community. They said the state government’s advice was to leave the dead birds in place, although council had begun removing some where “unacceptable public amenity or safety risks have been identified”.

Prof Rob Harcourt, at Macquarie University, said elephant seals like Sammy were “characters” and “the most gregarious animals you’ve ever seen”, which explained why communities named them.

Along with Sammy, a regular visitor to Portland, and Neil in Tasmania, many others had gained notoriety, including Humphrey, a three-tonne celebrity who frequented New Zealand coastal towns in the 1980s.

Southern elephant seals breed in large colonies, especially on Macquarie Island, Harcourt said. But because they’re so large and need a lot of food, they disperse widely to feed, migrating over 1,000 kilometres.

They’re strong swimmers, but on land they “move along like caterpillars,” he said.

Seals and sea lions often share spaces with wild birds, placing them at risk of infection from H5 bird flu. In Victoria, more than 100 marine mammals have been reported to the emergency animal disease hotline this month, although none so far have been confirmed as positive cases.

Seals were also vulnerable because they’re “thigmotactic”, Harcourt said, which means they love to lie touching each other. They recognised one another through “nasal exchange”. “They sniff each other’s faces”, he said; “mothers recognise their pups by touching noses”.

Southern elephant seals, listed as vulnerable under federal environment laws, were at “very high risk” of H5 bird flu, according to a national assessment. The deadly strain killed more than 13,000 pups on Heard Island in 2025 and 2026.

Australian sea lions, listed as endangered, were a particular concern given their low numbers. “Sea lions are like the labradors of the sea. They’re friendly and playful, and they’re curious,” Harcourt said. “I will be totally and utterly devastated if we lose them.”

With so many birds suffering, volunteer wildlife carers from western Victoria travelled to Portland last weekend, in a bid to humanely euthanise birds, which were being left to die slow, painful deaths.

“This is a Band-Aid over a bleeding wound,” David Mould from the Victorian Wildlife Alliance said. “This is not a solution. This is a couple of volunteers picking up the slack of what should be a major government operation.”

“The decline is rapid. These birds can’t fly. They have neurological symptoms,” he said. “They lose their ability to walk, and they start staggering around having seizures. You see them with their wings splayed out to support them off the ground, until they lose even the strength to do that.”

title: Nine CEO confident new AI laws will deliver a ‘world of growth in publishing’ as network slashes costs
excerpt:
Matt Stanton says company has ‘good pipeline’ of AI deals ahead even as it aims to cut $160m in costs

body_text:
Matt Stanton says company has ‘good pipeline’ of AI deals ahead even as it aims to cut $160m in costs

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The head of Nine Entertainment sees a “world of growth in publishing” on the horizon backed by laws designed to force tech platforms into commercial deals, even as the network cuts costs across its newsrooms.

Parliament passed revamped media bargaining laws last week, clearing the way for levies on global tech platforms that fail to strike deals with Australian news outlets for the use of their journalism.

Nine’s chief executive officer, Matt Stanton, told analysts on Wednesday he expected platforms such as Google and Facebook owner Meta to contribute amounts comparable to those under their previous arrangement, struck in 2021.

“There’s a number of variables that fly around, not just in news media bargaining, but yes, there is a world of growth in publishing,” Stanton said.

He said Nine also had a “good pipeline” of AI deals coming through after recently signing an agreement allowing Microsoft’s Copilot to access content.

The upbeat outlook comes at a challenging time for the broadcaster and publisher, which is stripping out more than $160m in costs over a three-year period as it revamps its business.

Nine recently announced a redundancy program at its Sydney Morning Herald and the Age newsrooms after the metropolitan mastheads were hit by a prolonged, weak advertising market.

Nine’s business masthead, the Australian Financial Review, has been spared the cuts and remains a robust revenue earner, according to financial results for the year to 30 June released on Wednesday.

Nine reported broadly flat revenue streams from its publishing arm, and a small decline from its streaming and broadcast unit, despite a record result for Stan. Nine’s television network has been weighed down by a weak advertising market.

Stanton said the company was focusing on “growth assets”, which include its newly acquired digital outdoor media company QMS, while it reduces exposure to “structurally challenged and smaller assets”.

Nine recorded a full-year net profit result of $142m from continuing businesses.

title: Trump-endorsed candidate clears key hurdle in red state gubernatorial race
excerpt: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secures a significant victory over incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary runoff, fueled by President Donald Trump's endorsement. Political strategis...
body_text:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton secures a significant victory over incumbent Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary runoff, fueled by President Donald Trump's endorsement. Political strategist Cassie Smedile emphasizes the enduring power of Trump's support among the Republican base. Paxton is now preparing to challenge Democratic candidate James Talarico in the general election, highlighting the contentious political landscape in Texas.

Mike Mazzei, a former Oklahoma state senator and financial planner, won a primary election runoff on Tuesday evening with the backing of President Donald Trump to secure the GOP nomination for governor in Oklahoma.

Having beaten out Genter Drummond, the current Oklahoma attorney general, Mazzei is now the heavy favorite to become the Sooner State’s next governor. His win is also a political victory for outgoing Gov. Kevin Stitt, who has opposed Drummond for years.

Stitt and Drummond have sparred over lawsuits, pointed letters and public criticisms. At one point, Stitt even described Drummond as a "longtime political enemy" in a quote to local outlets.

TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SPARKS RUNOFF AGAINST POPULAR PROSECUTOR IN KEY GUBERNATORIAL RACE

Gov. Kevin Stitt, R-Okla., (left) and Oklahoma Attorney General Genter Drummond disagree on whether the First Amendment allows the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board to grant St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Charter School public funding. (Getty/AP)

The feud between them centers on Drummond’s attacks of Oklahoma poultry companies for what he sees as decades of phosphorus pollution in water supplies. Stitt has rebuffed those characterizations, calling them an overreach of Drummond’s role as attorney general and warning that litigation against the companies could threaten jobs and the agricultural industry of the state.

Stitt endorsed Mazzei, stating that "we want a pro-business governor in there to take the lead for the next four years."

Stitt is prevented by term limits from running again. His exit prompted a crowded field of hopefuls to replace him, but after an initial primary on June 2, no candidate secured the 50% support needed to lock up the nomination outright.

Only Drummond and Mazzei advanced to a runoff.

Like Stitt, President Donald Trump also endorsed Mazzei, calling him a "MAGA warrior."

"As a successful Businessman, and former Chairman of the State Senate Finance Committee, and later, as Oklahoma’s Secretary of Budget, Mike knows the AMERICA FIRST Policies required to Grow our Economy, Create GREAT Jobs, Cut Taxes and Regulations, Promote MADE IN THE U.S.A., and Unleash American Energy DOMINANCE," Trump wrote in a May post to Truth Social.

TRUMP-BACKED FIREBRAND WINS ARIZONA GOP GOVERNOR PRIMARY, SETTING UP HIGH-STAKES SHOWDOWN

President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. Trump hosted the Rose Garden event to celebrate the administration's efforts on school choice. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Mazzei based his campaign on promises to cut taxes, among other state-government reforms.

"I have a detailed plan to eliminate Oklahoma’s income tax in six years. I have a plan to eliminate property taxes for seniors and veterans," Mazzei said in a campaign video posted to Instagram.

In addition to tax reforms, Mazzei highlighted preventing foreign nationals from buying up state land, bolstering the Oklahoma education system and government spending accountability.

In turn, Mazzei tried to paint Drummond as a fake Republican with a penchant for expanding government.

"His solution to every problem is to raise taxes and grow government," Mazzei said.

"He doesn’t understand money and finance. Crunching numbers is a skill you pick up when you earn your wealth rather than inherit it."

In his own campaign, Drummond, a multigenerational rancher and former fighter pilot, highlighted his record as attorney general. On his website, he touted having confronted Chinese criminal operations growing illegal marijuana farms, shutting down thousands of their illegal grow operations and enforcing immigration law.

"As a tough-on-crime attorney general and decorated fighter pilot, I have proven I will always fight for our freedom and defend our values," Drummond said in a campaign video.

TRUMP SWITCHES SUPPORT IN OKLAHOMA CONGRESSIONAL RACE AS FORMERLY ENDORSED PASTOR CANDIDATE SUSPENDS CAMPAIGN

Oklahoma state lawmaker Mike Mazzei gestures to reporters. (Nathan Fish/IMAGN)

"I’ll keep standing strong with President Trump to secure the border, deport illegals and stop the flow of drugs and crime," Drummond said.

The Club for Growth, a pro-small-government group that advocates for lower taxes and free-market principles and contributed $9 million in support of Mazzei, praised his win.

"Mike Mazzei is a principled conservative who will advocate for lower taxes, fewer regulations, and for Oklahoma parents to have a voice in their children’s education," Club for Growth PAC President David McIntosh said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Meanwhile, Gentner Drummond has spent his career putting radical education bureaucrats ahead of families by opposing school freedom. The message is clear, if you oppose school freedom and call yourself a Republican, expect to lose your next primary."

Having cleared the primary, Mazzei will face off against Democratic nominee Cyndi Munson, House minority leader in the Oklahoma House of Representatives. The general election is set for Nov. 3.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump endorsement boosts sister of late Lindsey Graham to historic runoff victory
excerpt:
Darline Graham speaks at election night headquarters in Columbia, South Carolina, as votes are counted in the historic GOP runoff to keep her late brother's Senate seat.

A powerful name and an endors...
body_text:
Darline Graham speaks at election night headquarters in Columbia, South Carolina, as votes are counted in the historic GOP runoff to keep her late brother's Senate seat.

A powerful name and an endorsement from President Donald Trump proved more than enough to score an unlikely candidate a win in the latest runoff election in South Carolina.

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., toppled Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., in a whirlwind race to replace her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, as the GOP nominee for the Senate after his sudden death in July.

Just a little over a month after his death at 71 years old, South Carolinians opted to stick with a familiar name in Graham, who despite having little political experience prior to her appointment to finish out the remainder of her brother’s term, scored Trump’s coveted endorsement.

DARLINE GRAHAM FACES MAKE-OR-BREAK GOP RUNOFF IN HISTORIC BID TO KEEP BROTHER’S SENATE SEAT

Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., listens to a question at a campaign event at Holt Bros BBQ in Florence, S.C., on Aug. 19, 2026. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)

Though her appointment by South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster was viewed as temporary, Trump pushed her to run beyond the five months left in her brother’s term.

"Darline is somebody I've known for a long time," Trump said during a rally for her in Myrtle Beach last week. "I asked her to do this. I said, ‘Darline, you got to do it,’ because everyone loves her. Everyone respects her."

"So I've known her through Lindsey — I've known her for so long," he continued. "I think Lindsey respected Darline more than any other person he knows, including me."

LINDSEY GRAHAM’S SISTER ADMITS SHE’S ‘NOT THAT INFORMED ON NATIONAL SECURITY’ WHILE SEEKING FULL SENATE TERM

And Trump sent in last-minute financial reinforcements to help her, following a gaffe during her final debate with Norman when she admitted that she had little knowledge of the strategic importance of Taiwan.

Graham has styled herself as a much different politician than her brother, focused more on domestic issues than foreign.

Trump's mammoth, $400 million campaign war chest through MAGA Inc., which has largely been untapped this cycle despite a handful of Senate races shifting in power dynamics across the country, dumped over $800,000 into a phone campaign in support of Graham over the weekend, according to campaign finance records.

While Graham styled herself as a more home front than abroad focused candidate, she made one thing clear through debates and limited campaign time: a vote for her was a vote for the Trump agenda.

RALPH NORMAN SUGGESTS SPECIAL GOP PRIMARY RUNOFF RIVAL DARLINE GRAHAM IS THE ESTABLISHMENT'S CHOSEN CANDIDATE

President Donald Trump leaves the stage after speaking at a campaign rally with Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., on Aug. 21, 2026, in Myrtle Beach, S.C. (Getty Images)

She targeted Norman for bucking House Republican leadership, and, at times, Trump, but noted, "We already have enough problem Democrats, we don’t need a problem Republican."

And though she’s only been in the Senate for a handful of weeks, Graham argued to voters that she’d done more than Norman had in his entire congressional career, touting the passage of the long-awaited bipartisan Russia sanctions package initially pushed by her brother, but at times slowed by the White House.

"I was in Washington for only two weeks before I passed the Russia and Iran Sanctions Act through the Senate," Graham said. "I then passed the deciding vote to confirm President Trump's attorney general, Todd Blanche."

"Simply put, I've done more in 20 days than Ralph Norman has done in 20 years."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Democratic newcomer scores runoff upset in Oklahoma, vows to impeach Trump if elected
excerpt:
Rep. John James, R-Mich., joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's controversial comments and state charges against noncitizens who voted.

A political newcome...
body_text:
Rep. John James, R-Mich., joins 'Saturday in America' to discuss Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed's controversial comments and state charges against noncitizens who voted.

A political newcomer just scored a victory in ruby-red Oklahoma, and, if elected, she would put all her energy into impeaching President Donald Trump.

N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas, a nurse who has never run for office before, bested Jim Priest, a lawyer and nonprofit executive, in the runoff race for the Democratic Senate nomination in Oklahoma. Thomas, though a new face, scored the highest percentage of votes in the June primary contest that featured five total candidates vying for the nomination.

It tees up a battle against history in Oklahoma, where voters haven’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in more than three decades.

PRIMARY TAKEAWAYS: DEMS’ LEFT-CENTER BATTLE INTENSIFIES AS SCHUMER TAKES ANOTHER HIT; SPLIT DECISION FOR TRUMP

President Donald Trump speaks during an event in the Rose Garden of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

And Thomas, who lists a host of policy proposals on her campaign website, including beefing up teacher pay, restoring Roe v. Wade, and expanding Obamacare, among other boilerplate Democratic proposals, also wants to accomplish one thing in the early days of her Senate career: impeaching Trump.

During an interview with NPR affiliate KOSU last month, Thomas was asked about the Republican nominee, Rep. Kevin Hern, R-Okla., and his "fierce" backing of Trump, and how, if elected, she would approach a working relationship with the president.

"Like I said, I'm kind, not nice. So I will make sure that I work as diligently as I can to make sure that within my first 100 days that we impeach, remove and convict," Thomas said. "They will have to pry that pen out of my cold, dead hands before I go any further with allowing this administration to continue doing what they're doing."

DEM SENATE CANDIDATE CALLS TO 'SHUT THE WHITE HOUSE DOWN,' IMPEACH 2 SUPREME COURT JUSTICES

"So, I mean, hopefully that's a good answer," she continued. "But I am going to remove, impeach, remove and convict. That's it. Like that's all. That's the answer."

First, she’d have to survive Election Night in November against Hern, a tall task given that Trump won Oklahoma by nearly 35 points in 2024.

Though Thomas has pulled off two underdog performances, earning roughly 45% of the vote during her first go-round for the Democratic nomination and then defeating Priest with no political experience, Hern is a different matter.

DARLINE GRAHAM FACES MAKE-OR-BREAK GOP RUNOFF IN HISTORIC BID TO KEEP BROTHER’S SENATE SEAT

Rep. Kevin Hern, R-Okla., talks with reporters outside the U.S. Capitol on Sept. 11, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc.)

He’s amassed an impressive campaign war chest that at one point peaked at nearly $10 million so far this cycle. Thomas, however, has raised just shy of $60,000.

He also boasts the endorsement of Trump and has touted his desire to pass the president’s biggest policy priority, the SAVE America Act.

Hern noted in a statement to Fox News Digital that Oklahomans "love President Trump and the America First Agenda."

"Socialist Democrats like N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas are wildly out of touch with the values of Oklahomans and the direction they want our country moving toward," Hern said. "President Trump and Republicans are focused on delivering results. N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas and the radical left are focused on partisan politics against a president Oklahomans overwhelmingly elected."

Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Is Sudan’s battlefield shaping the terms of its next political phase?
excerpt: Sudan’s war is showing signs of a changing dynamic. Sudanese armed forces (SAF) have made a series of gains in North Kordofan state; the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces (RSF) is facing a new w...
body_text:
Sudan’s war is showing signs of a changing dynamic. Sudanese armed forces (SAF) have made a series of gains in North Kordofan state; the paramilitary group Rapid Support Forces (RSF) is facing a new wave of defections; and army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is opening a political track while insisting the military campaign will continue.

Army advances are putting pressure on RSF supply lines; defections are raising questions about the force’s cohesion; and al-Burhan, who also heads the Transitional Sovereignty Council, is seeking to shape a political process from a position strengthened by developments on the battlefield.

But the wider battlefield remains contested. Together, the military pressure, defections and political outreach point to a potentially important shift: battlefield developments may be starting to affect the political balance.

The clearest recent gains have come in North Kordofan, a state in central Sudan that links the capital, Khartoum, with the country’s western regions.

In late July, the army announced that it had retaken Bara, Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Sayala, along with other positions in the state. Al Jazeera reported that the advances also secured the national Exports Road, a key route linking Khartoum, through Omdurman, with el-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan.

The gains do not amount to control of the wider Kordofan region. But they have significance beyond the territory captured.

The army’s control of the Exports Road has strengthened its position in North Kordofan and added pressure on RSF supply lines. Al Jazeera reported on August 21 that the army was continuing efforts to cut those supply lines as fighting expanded across Kordofan, Darfur and the Blue Nile region.

The battlefield pressure has coincided with a marked increase in defections from the RSF.

On August 20, the army announced that about 318 people, including four officers, had joined its ranks, arriving in Northern state in about 50 combat vehicles before moving to Omdurman. Al Jazeera also reported separate groups from Kordofan and Khartoum, including 270 people, among them 21 field commanders, as well as 45 fighters and commanders from the Bara area who surrendered to the army.

The numbers alone do not tell the story. The timing does.

Al Jazeera’s August 21 analysis links the growing defections to several factors, including battlefield developments, internal problems within the RSF, social and tribal dynamics, and pressure created by the army’s advances and efforts to disrupt RSF supply lines. It also notes that the trend does not by itself mean the RSF is collapsing.

If the trend continues, it could become increasingly significant, particularly if more commanders and fighters conclude that the battlefield balance is shifting against the RSF.

For now, the more cautious conclusion is that battlefield pressure may be affecting the RSF’s cohesion without yet amounting to a broader breakdown of the organisation.

The SAF chief’s political initiative is unfolding alongside these military developments.

On August 15, he announced that the state would provide temporary immunity and legal, political and security guarantees to participants in a national dialogue managed by an independent national mechanism. Criminal proceedings against participants facing charges would be suspended during their involvement in the dialogue, without removing the rights of those who had filed complaints.

Al-Burhan said the initiative came from a group of Sudanese who had approached him with a proposal for dialogue. He said the group would independently manage the process and that the state would not determine its agenda or outcomes. He also said he had begun engaging with national forces that had supported the state and its institutions, with the aim of involving them in completing state institutions, including a legislative council.

But this is not a move away from the war.

Al-Burhan said he would not accept what he called a “peace without substance” that would bring RSF commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, also known as Hemedti, and his supporters to power. He also said the path to peace begins with the RSF leaving cities and being gathered in designated areas.

On August 21, Al Jazeera reported that al-Burhan said the fighting would continue until what he described as the rebellion was ended, while the army was working to cut RSF supply lines. He also rejected a truce that would allow the RSF to reorganise, while saying he remained open to a just peace and national dialogue that excluded the RSF.

Al-Burhan is therefore not choosing between war and politics. He is pursuing both, maintaining military pressure while opening a political process he says should preserve the state and its institutions.

Malik Agar, deputy chairman of the Transitional Sovereignty Council, has made the government’s position even clearer.

In an interview with Al Jazeera on August 22, Agar said the current option was military resolution unless serious conditions for negotiations emerged. He said the RSF would have to withdraw from cities and residential areas before negotiations could begin, stressing that the government remained open to initiatives that preserve Sudan’s unity and state institutions.

In a separate Al Jazeera interview published on August 23, Agar said the army would win but that the war would ultimately end through negotiations.

He argued that Sudan’s crisis was rooted in deeper problems, including the weakness of the state and the failure of political elites to manage the country’s ethnic, cultural, religious and geographic diversity.

His position reflects the government’s broader calculation: maintain military pressure while leaving the door open to negotiations from a stronger position on the battlefield.

The army’s gains in North Kordofan have strengthened its position along a strategically important route. The growing defections from the RSF are raising questions about the force’s cohesion. At the same time, the RSF remains active on several fronts, and the wider battlefield remains contested.

That combination gives the recent developments significance beyond individual battles or defections. The changing military balance may now be beginning to shape the terms of Sudan’s next political phase.

For al-Burhan, the potential advantage is not simply territorial. If military pressure continues to produce defections and weaken RSF cohesion, it could give the SAF greater room to shape who participates in a political process and the conditions under which future negotiations take place.

For the RSF, the challenge is therefore not only to hold territory. It is to prevent battlefield pressure from becoming an internal crisis of cohesion.

That has not happened yet. Military setbacks do not automatically translate into political marginalisation.

The army’s recent gains are best understood not as evidence of a decisive victory, but as a shift in the conditions under which the next phase of the war may be fought, and eventually negotiated.

Can the RSF contain the defections and preserve its bargaining position, or will continued military pressure give al-Burhan greater leverage in Sudan’s next political phase?

title: Australia news live: inflation eases less than expected, making rate rise likelier; NT MP Luke Gosling stands aside as envoy
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Inflation has dropped to 3.5% in the year to July, from 3.8%, as fuel prices rebounded in the month and building costs jumped.

The headlin...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Inflation has dropped to 3.5% in the year to July, from 3.8%, as fuel prices rebounded in the month and building costs jumped.

The headline rate was down but came in substantially stronger than economists had predicted, with the consensus forecast for inflation to drop to 3.2%.

The ABS data also showed the Reserve Bank’s preferred measure of underlying inflation also holding at 3.6%, rather than moderating to 3.5% as had been expected.

The cost of home building was the largest contributor to the annual headline inflation rate, climbing by 5% in the year, while grocery prices climbed by 3.2%.

Financial markets ahead of the latest consumer price data were pricing in a roughly 60% chance of an RBA interest rate hike by December, and this morning’s figures make another rate increase more likely.

Victorian treasurer defends public transport levy

The Victorian treasurer, Colin Brooks, held a press conference earlier this morning – just minutes after a report by the state’s auditor general revealed the government has been secretly charging public transport users extra to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop.

The report into the first stage of the SRL – from Cheltenham to Box Hill – revealed the government added a 1% levy on public transport fares on top of existing adjustments in line with inflation on 1 January 2025 but did not inform Victorians.

The auditor general said 60% of the revenue earned will go to SRL East but the levy has not been named as one of the government’s value capture methods for the project.

Brooks told reporters that’s because “it’s not part of the value capture framework that we’re using for SRL”. He went on:

double quotation markSuburban Rail Loop East has a very clear funding model – three components: value capture, state government, and the federal government. In terms of the value capture framework, the charge that you’re talking about is not part of that framework.

He said revenue from the levy was “going back into public transport infrastructure, and services across the state” not just SRL East.

Brooks however admitted the government “could have been more transparent about how we’re investing that money”:

double quotation markI say this genuinely, the auditor general plays a really important function in terms of providing government with advice, and so they’ve highlighted the fact that this charge we’re not we haven’t been really transparent around where this is being spent.

He said he didn’t know when it was approved and first learnt about it – despite being treasurer for four weeks – when he read the report.

Silence has hung over a picturesque police station as hundreds stood in respect to mark one year since two officers were gunned down by Dezi Freeman, AAP reports.

It was on 26 August 2025 when detective leading senior constable Neal Thompson and senior constable Vadim de Waart-Hottart and eight other officers went to Freeman’s remote home in Victoria’s high country.

After attempting to serve a warrant to Freeman at the Porepunkah property, 310km north-east of Melbourne, the two officers were shot dead and a third officer was left seriously injured, sparking a huge manhunt for the killer.

On Wednesday morning, a minute’s silence was held at Bright police station, where more than 400 police officers and family members filled the crowd.

Heartfelt tributes punctuated the hour-long service, with tributes delivered and officers reflecting on their time working alongside the pair.

Lois Kirk and Dianne Thompson, the sisters of Thompson, said the past year had been very difficult.

double quotation markWe miss our big brother every single day. Neal was fiercely loyal, a natural leader and just as tough as he was soft. It’s what made him such a good police officer. He followed in the footsteps of our grandfather and never wanted to be anything else. He truly loved his job.

Melons from Japanese PM valued at $200 each, government documents reveal

Anthony Albanese’s department confirmed the Japanese crown melons he received from Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, were valued at $200 each, explaining why they weren’t declared on the prime minister’s register of interests.

Documents provided to the Senate by Albanese’s assistant minister, Patrick Gorman, reveal official government gift records cataloguing the receipt of four Japanese melons – two handed over directly from Takaichi to Albanese on her visit to Canberra in May, and then another two apparently delivered to the Lodge via the Japanese embassy in June.

Each of the four melons was valued at $200, according to the gift documents shared with the Senate.

They later, of course, were at the centre of the so-called “melongate” controversy following Albanese’s description of the gift on the Bush Deep podcast.

The PM, in the podcast, described the melon gift as “pretty strange but ended up being quite good” – and he must have enjoyed them in the end, because all four were “retained by recipient”, the documents state.

The first two were given directly by Takaichi during the dinner, according to the documents, with another two handed to the Department of PM&C from the Japanese embassy, then later dropped off at the Lodge.

The documents were obtained after a request from One Nation senator Sean Bell, with the documents later uploaded on to the parliament’s website.

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson had questioned why the melons weren’t declared on Albanese’s parliamentary register of interests, alongside other gifts he received from Takaichi. But the departmental records show each gift of two melons, valued at $200 for each individual fruit, came to $400 all up – below the threshold for declaring gifts, which is $750.

Further to the news just now that federal Labor MP Luke Gosling has stepped aside from his special envoy role, you can read more on the background to that, and the charges laid against him, here:

Northern Territory Labor MP Luke Gosling has stood aside as Anthony Albanese’s special envoy for veterans and northern Australia, a day after police charged him with one count of breaching bail conditions.

He is fighting charges from July, when he was arrested over the alleged assault of the territory’s administrator, David Connolly.

Gosling was charged with two counts of assault over an incident that allegedly occurred at a cultural festival in Darwin last month.

Albanese and Gosling had resisted pressure for him to stand aside from the envoy role, which is not part of the federal ministry.

double quotation markDue to the ongoing media attention and the distraction that this is causing to the business of government, I have decided to temporarily stand aside as special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and Northern Australia, until these matters have been heard.

Inflation has dropped to 3.5% in the year to July, from 3.8%, as fuel prices rebounded in the month and building costs jumped.

The headline rate was down but came in substantially stronger than economists had predicted, with the consensus forecast for inflation to drop to 3.2%.

The ABS data also showed the Reserve Bank’s preferred measure of underlying inflation also holding at 3.6%, rather than moderating to 3.5% as had been expected.

The cost of home building was the largest contributor to the annual headline inflation rate, climbing by 5% in the year, while grocery prices climbed by 3.2%.

Financial markets ahead of the latest consumer price data were pricing in a roughly 60% chance of an RBA interest rate hike by December, and this morning’s figures make another rate increase more likely.

Roberts ‘in two minds’ about whether gay people should be equal

One Nation’s Malcolm Roberts told a conference earlier this year that he was in “two minds” about whether gay people should have equal rights.

In footage from June’s Church and State conference, released on Sunday, the senator can be seen responding to a question about James Ashby, the party’s director, who is gay.

Both Roberts and the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, appeared at the conservative Christian conference.

In the footage, Roberts described Ashby as bright, honest and straight.

Asylum Seeker Resource Centre reflects on the Tampa affair, 25 years on

The Asylum Seeker Resource Centre says Australia remains locked in a “distorted debate” about immigration, 25 years on from the Tampa freighter that launched a new era of migration policies in the country.

Kon Karapanagiotidis, the ASRC’s founder, said in a statement:

double quotation markPolitics poisons policy, and there is no greater example than Australia’s treatment of people seeking asylum. Twenty-five years ago, Tampa presented Australia with a choice: meet people rescued at sea with humanity and protection, or choose fear. Our political leaders chose fear, and we have been living with the consequences ever since.

Tampa didn’t just change refugee policy. It changed Australian politics.

double quotation mark25 years later, we still hear the same drumbeat of fear. Inflammatory headlines. Migration reduced to numbers. People seeking asylum turned into political problems. We deserve better than another generation of this politics.

Guardian Australia’s Ben Doherty detailed the Tampa affair in a piece on its 20th anniversary in 2021. Take a look:

Australia’s largest locally owned media group has lifted its annual earnings as it continues to focus on its streaming and broadcast assets, including Stan, 9Now and digital publishing, AAP reports.

Nine Entertainment, which also owns 9 Network and major mastheads such as The Sydney Morning Herald, The Age and the Australian Financial Review, said those divisions were expected to contribute more than 60% of its revenue in the new financial year.

The group made a 2025-26 bottom line net profit of $510.6m, on a consolidated basis, up from $133.3m in the previous year ended 30 June. Chief executive Matt Stanton said:

double quotation markWe will continue to invest in premium content and focus on opportunities to maximise the reach and commercialisation of that content, whilst continuing to explore technology initiatives that help to expedite growth opportunities.

Commissioner to delay final report into antisemitism to allow for commemorations of Bondi attack

Commissioner Virginia Bell will delay – but only by four days – the handing down of her final report into antisemitism and social cohesion, in order not to distract from commemorations of the Bondi attack.

On the last day of public hearings of the commission, Bell resisted a public push to extend the commission’s work by several months, in order to hear from more witnesses.

Bell said the letters patent for the royal commission stated her final report should be handed to government on 14 December 2027, the first anniversary of the Bondi terror attack.

She said she had noted the push, including from Jewish community leaders and parliamentarians, to extend the timeframe of her commission, but that the commission had worked hard to address all of its terms of reference “in accordance with that timetable, and I do not seek any meaningful extension of it”.

double quotation markAmong other considerations, I note the evidence that has been given by senior public officials that the implementation of important policy proposals is awaiting the recommendations of this Commission.

But the commissioner said she did not want the release of the report to distract from commemorations.

double quotation markThe 14th of December is the anniversary of the massacre. It will be a solemn occasion marked by memorials. I’m aware of concern within the Jewish community that delivery of the report on the anniversary would be a distraction. I fully understand that concern and to avoid that distraction I have asked for a short extension of the term with a view to the submission of my final report on Friday the 18th of December.

Woolworths won’t run Ooshies promotion year-round

Supermarket giant Woolworths says it won’t be running Ooshies giveaways more regularly despite the success of this year’s campaign.

Customers received the blind bags of plastic Disney characters for every $30 they spent at Woolworths from mid-July to mid-August, the latest such campaign from the company. Its annual results today reported they boosted Woolworths’ sales growth by up to 2% compared to the same period in 2025.

Group chief executive Amanda Bardwell told reporters today the campaign had attracted shoppers who wouldn’t normally visit Woolworths. She said:

double quotation markWe see some customers who certainly might decide to add a few more items to their basket while they’re shopping with us so that they certainly qualify for the extra Ooshie. And then we do have some customers who might not shop with us very frequently, who choose to switch to Woolies during that period.

Bardwell said the promotions offered a “great opportunity to go beyond the routine shopping experience and create that real surprise, delight, community moment”.

But asked if Woolworths would capitalise on that momentum, Bardwell said:

double quotation markAs we move forward, collectibles will continue to be part of our offer, but we don’t offer them 365 days of the year. … we don’t think we need to be running them all the time.

The Victorian government secretly increased public transport fares to raise money to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop and other Big Build projects, an auditor general report tabled in parliament this morning reveals.

The report found the government’s plan to fund the first stage of the multibillion dollar project, dubbed SRL East, lacked transparency, and “some funding sources are uncertain”. This includes its target of generating a third of project costs through revenue raising measures.

The auditor general revealed one revenue raising measure: a levy on all public transport fares in metropolitan Melbourne and regional Victoria, which the government has used to help fund SRL East and other Big Build projects since 2025.

However, the government has not made this public. The report reads:

double quotation markThe government and Transport Victoria did not acknowledge the new public transport fare levy in their public communications about the 2025 and 2026 annual fare increases. As at June 2026, they still have not announced it.

The report also questions whether it will be completed by 2035, given the project has already “experienced significant delays” of up to six months on early works and station contracts are yet to be awarded. It also said the “on the evidence available to date” the project is “more likely than not to exceed its publicly disclosed cost of up to $34.5bn”.

Future Fund boss steps down after bumper year

Raphael Arndt has announced he will step down as the CEO of the Future Fund, as the $290bn sovereign wealth fund reported a bumper 14.8% return for the past financial year.

Arndt has been at the fund for almost two decades – essentially since it was set up in 2006 to help pay for the public pension liabilities of government workers.

He has been CEO for the past six years and before that spent the same time as the chief investment officer. Arndt will stay on until the end of the year as they look for a successor, and after that will return to the private sector.

Separately, the Future Fund reported a 10-year return of 9% per annum, beating its target of 7.1%.

Greg Combet, the chair of the Future Fund board of guardians, said 2025-26 was one of the best years in its history.

double quotation markThis result has also been achieved while investing in national priority sectors with the board having now committed around $3.5bn of new investment into domestic housing, infrastructure and the energy transition. The Future Fund now has almost $20bn of investment in domestic infrastructure held in our portfolio.

Sydney Harbour tunnel partially closed after car fire

The Sydney Harbour tunnel remains partially closed after a car fire, Transport for NSW says.

Officials said the tunnel was initially closed in both directions, but northbound traffic is now open. Southbound traffic remains closed and traffic to the city is being diverted to the Harbour Bridge.

Motorists are encouraged to allow plenty of extra time for travel, and buses are also delayed.

An air charter company has confirmed one of its light planes has crashed into the sea off a remote island, with fears held for the pilot as a maritime search continues, AAP reports.

Air Frontier says its twin-engined Beechcraft Baron aircraft went missing just before midday on Tuesday after taking off from Gove airport at Nhulunbuy on the Northern Territory coast with only the pilot aboard.

It was due to land at the remote Indigenous community of Numbulwar at 11.50am but never arrived.

A search led by NT police began after a witness on a vessel reported seeing the plane crash into the sea near Isle Woodah. In a statement on Tuesday evening police said no aircraft wreckage or persons had yet been located.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau has been notified of the crash and has initiated an investigation.

Woolworths’ net profit has boomed 18% to $1.14bn as customers face cost-of-living pressures, the company has reported.

Supermarket sales were up 4.6% in the year to June, its annual results today show. Sales have accelerated since the start of July as the company brought in its Ooshies collectibles promotion, to run 7.6% above the prior year. The company estimates the Ooshies program alone accounted for about a quarter of that growth rate.

The Australian supermarkets division increased the profit margin on its earnings from to 5.5%, from 5.3%. Its pre-tax earnings rose $232m to exceed $2.95bn.

Woolworth’s strong result was helped by Big W returning to profit in the year, with pre-tax earnings of $64m, from a $33m loss the year before. But the department store chain has seen its sales decline in the last eight weeks, despite its inclusion in the Ooshies program.

Woolworths attributed the drop to “ongoing cost-of-living pressures on households, particularly budget customers and weaker trade in the Everyday business”.

title: Dolly Parton refused to pick political sides for decades: ‘I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer’
excerpt:
‘America Reports’ co-anchor John Roberts announces the death of country music star Dolly Parton at the age of 80.

Dolly Parton spent decades singing about love, heartbreak, faith and working "9 to 5,...
body_text:
‘America Reports’ co-anchor John Roberts announces the death of country music star Dolly Parton at the age of 80.

Dolly Parton spent decades singing about love, heartbreak, faith and working "9 to 5," but there was one arena the country music legend repeatedly resisted entering: partisan politics.

"I am not political, and I refuse to get caught up in political things," Parton told USA Today in a 2020 interview.

Parton, who died Tuesday at 80, maintained that position through the presidential elections, pointed questions about President Donald Trump, offers of the nation's highest civilian honor and controversies involving some of her fellow entertainers.

KENNY CHESNEY TELLS BILL MAHER THE KEY REASON HE REFUSES TO TELL HIS LISTENERS HOW TO VOTE

Dolly Parton passed away peacefully on Tuesday. (Shirlaine Forrest/WireImage)

"I don't like to get involved in politics, because first of all, I have as many Republican fans as I do Democrats," Parton told USA Today. "I don't want to offend anybody, I have a right to myself."

"Like God gave us free will, America gave us free speech, but you've got to be responsible for anything you say and do," she added.

Two years earlier, Parton was repeatedly pressed about Trump during an interview with ABC's David Wright, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel.

DWAYNE 'THE ROCK' JOHNSON REJECTS HOLLYWOOD’S POLITICAL OBSESSION, BLASTS CELEBRITY ATTACK CULTURE

Dolly Parton attends the "Dolly: An Original Musical" fireside chat and press conference at The Fisher Center for the Performing Arts, Jan. 28, 2025 in Nashville, Tenn. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

"I have a lot of fans out there, and I don’t want to offend anybody," Parton said.

When Wright attempted to draw a parallel between Trump and the sexually abusive boss in Parton's 1980 film "9 to 5," she refused to bite.

"I’m not addressing that," Parton said. "I learned a long time ago, keep your damn mouth shut if you want to stay in show business. … I’m not in politics, I’m an entertainer."

When Wright pointed out that Parton was also a role model, she responded: "Yes I am. That’s why I don’t talk about people."

JOHNNY CARSON'S FRIEND SAYS LATE-NIGHT KING WISELY AVOIDED PARTISANSHIP AS KIMMEL CONTROVERSY GROWS

Dolly Parton appears on the Phil Donahue Show at WGN Television in Chicago, on April 30, 1977. (Getty Images)

Parton's determination to avoid partisan politics with one of America's highest honors.

She revealed in 2021 that the Trump administration had twice offered her the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Parton said she declined the first offer because her husband, Carl Dean, was ill and the second because she would not travel during the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the BBC.

By then, the Biden administration had also approached her about the award. "Now I feel like if I take it, it'll be doing politics, so I'm not so sure," Parton told NBC's "Today."

MICK JAGGER DOESN'T WANT TO 'LECTURE' FANS, SAYS HIS JOB IS TO MAKE PEOPLE 'HAVE THE BEST TIME'

Parton wowed the crowd when performing at Glastonbury in 2014. (Jim Dyson/Getty Images)

Her aversion to political camps did not mean she kept quiet about everything she believed.

"I know whatever I say, people are going to listen, and they’re going to make more of it than maybe what I meant. So I have to be careful," Parton told People in 2021. "Of course I have my opinion, but I’m not an opinionated person as a rule. You’re allowed your own beliefs and your own faith, but you don’t have to use it like a weapon when it could be a tool."

Parton's political neutrality was something she could joke about.

"My daddy was a Republican, my mama was a Democrat, and I’m a hypocrite!" Parton famously quipped, pronouncing 'hypocrite' as 'hypo-crat' in her iconic Tennessee drawl.

Country singer Dolly Parton in 1970. (Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images)

Parton's philosophy was tested again when she recorded a duet with Kid Rock for her 2023 album, "Rockstar."

Parton defended working with the conservative musician after she was questioned about the collaboration, telling The Hollywood Reporter that she had recorded the song before a controversy involving Kid Rock but would likely have worked with him anyway, according to Rolling Stone.

"Hey, just because I love you don’t mean I don’t love Kid Rock. Just because I love Kid Rock don’t mean I don’t love you," Parton said. "I don’t condemn or criticize. I just accept and love."

Parton said she still would "probably" have recorded the duet because she considered Kid Rock talented and believed accepting someone did not require agreeing with everything they did.

BILLY RAY CYRUS URGES PRAYER FOR TRUMP, SAYS BEING COMMANDER IN CHIEF IS A 'TOUGH JOB'

Dolly Parton was one of the Kennedy Center Honorees in 2006 under former President George W. Bush. (Scott Suchman/WireImage)

"I think that’s terrible," Parton said, according to Rolling Stone. "We all make mistakes. We don’t all get caught at it."

Parton tied that belief to her Christian faith, arguing that people deserved forgiveness and second chances.

"I ask God every day to let Him shine through me. He’s given me that gift to be able to talk to them, and I’m very careful with it. And people don’t really come to see me be me — they come to see me be them, the parts of me they can relate to," she told People in 2021.

During the 2016 presidential campaign, Parton clarified that she had not endorsed Hillary Clinton after comments she made about the Democratic nominee were interpreted as an endorsement, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel.

Asked later about the race between Clinton and Trump, Parton jokingly called the campaign "the greatest show on television," and described both candidates as "nuts."

Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductee Dolly Parton performs onstage during attends the 37th Annual Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Induction Ceremony at Microsoft Theater, Nov. 5, 2022, in Los Angeles. (Kevin Mazur/Getty Images)

Even running for president herself wasn't entertained by the iconic entertainer for a moment.

"No. I don’t think anybody could actually do a great job at that," Parton told Metro in 2023, according to People. "I think we’ve had enough ‘boobs’ in the White House."

Parton said she preferred trying to make a difference through music and the way she treated others.

"I’m not smart enough to be in politics, or maybe I’m too smart," she said. "Either way, I’m not qualified for that type of a job. But I’m pretty qualified to do what I do, which is to point people in the right direction, to write about it in songs or speak about things."

Parton died after a "brief battle with cancer," according to her representatives. At her request, a small, private service will be held for her immediate family, with the family asking for donations to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library rather than flowers.

Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: College athletics' latest mess: Court orders say athletes can play, but SEC and Big Ten ready to fight
excerpt:
Dan Dakich torches the NCAA for suspending Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for a plane ticket.

The college athletics world is reeling after the SEC and Big Ten created new guidelines governing the ...
body_text:
Dan Dakich torches the NCAA for suspending Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter for a plane ticket.

The college athletics world is reeling after the SEC and Big Ten created new guidelines governing the eligibility of athletes who planned to join teams this week following injunctions and temporary restraining orders granted by multiple judges.

On Tuesday, both conferences, who will soon be joined by the ACC and Big 12, voted to enact new rules that would prevent athletes who have participated in professional sports from reentering the college landscape.

The decision comes after players in several states were granted injunctions or temporary restraining orders allowing them to play this season.

Most of the lawsuits stem from the NCAA’s new eligibility guidelines, which give athletes five years to play five seasons of college athletics.

NCAA WINS TENTH CIRCUIT 'STAY', BUT FACES MORE ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FROM 2022 CLASS ATHLETES IN CHAOTIC TIME

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey and Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti meet with reporters during a joint press conference in Nashville, Tennessee (Trey Wallace/FOX NEWS)

Under the new policies, any athlete who has signed with a professional team, declared for the NFL Draft or participated in any type of professional training camp will be ineligible for conference competition.

But, there was one difference from a public standpoint with the SEC and Big Ten.

On Tuesday evening, SEC presidents and chancellors held a vote on how to move forward with the new guidelines pertaining to these ongoing cases revolving around athletes who have participated at the professional level in some form or fashion.

NCAA IGNORED THE WARNINGS. NOW IT'S FIGHTING FOR SURVIVAL IN COURTROOMS ACROSS AMERICA OVER ELIGIBILITY

In addition to the guidelines created by the SEC, the conference has also given Greg Sankey the power to enforce these rules, which include suspension of coaches and monetary fines to each school who violates them.

Big Ten Commissioner Tony Petitti speaks at Big Ten football media day at Lucas Oil Stadium on July 26, 2023 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Michael Hickey/Getty Images)

So, what does this mean for schools who are preparing to bring athletes onto campus for the upcoming college football or basketball season?

According to attorney Ryan Downton, who represents a number of players, the are currently "working on a legal strategy" on how to move forward against both the NCAA and participating conferences who have enacted these new guidelines.

"The SEC’s actions put the NCAA in contempt of multiple court orders," Downton told OutKick-Fox News on Tuesday night. "It is cartel-like conduct when NCAA conferences attempt to create their own spur of the moment rules in response to Courts enjoining those same rules at the NCAA level"

OLE MISS FILES LAWSUITS AGAINST COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYERS WHO LEFT FOR LANE KIFFIN'S LSU

Multiple sources told OutKick that the vote within the SEC was unanimous, though that does not mean there will not be legal action taken over the next few days.

"We are still working on a legal strategy," attorney Ryan Downton noted.

At the forefront of this fight, even though he was not the first coach or team to bring in a player who has in some way competed at the NFL level, is LSU coach Lane Kiffin.

Over the last few days, Kiffin has voiced his reasoning behind the recruitment of such athletes who have already gained NFL experience. Essentially, the Tigers coach mentioned that if he didn’t strike first, some other school would.

"So, you know, we have you know made a decision to recruit some kids around the country, and through these multiple injunctions around the country, which, this is not a first time in college sports, a group of players were granted a fifth year of eligibility, in multiple sports. And through them winning their injunction and entry into the portal, they’re available to recruit," Kiffin noted on Monday.

"So ourselves, like many places around the country, are recruiting them. At the end of the day, you know, because of these rulings, they’re either going to play for you or they’re going to play somewhere else around the country. So, we made a decision to recruit them, like probably most people are."

This includes former Ole Miss football players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris, who are both set to join the LSU roster thanks to a ruling from the 19th District Court of Louisiana that granted them an additional season of eligibility.

Dae'quan Wright catches a touchdown pass for Ole Miss against Miami during the College Football Playoff semifinal at the Vrbo Fiesta Bowl at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Jan. 8, 2026. Miami defeated Ole Miss 31-27. (Getty Images)

But, there have been plenty of others who have gone down this route, winning cases in state courts that allow them to return this season. Texas offensive lineman Cole Hutson is another, who sued the NCAA in a Texas court for an additional season.

Attorney Darren Heitner, who represents Dae'Quan Wright, told OutKick that the SEC should abide by the order granted by the 19th District Court of Louisiana.

"He should be rostered by LSU and be a great contributor for the Tigers. The SEC should heed the court order recently issued by a Louisiana judge," Heitner said.

The question is whether LSU, and others, will move forward in bringing in athletes knowing that it would be in violation of conference rules, but also legal in the eyes of the courts who have granted them injunctions.

Buckle up, this could get interesting over the next few days.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.
